Application information

The input and processing of the transliterated text has been done with TUSTEP, the
            Tuebingen System of Text--Processing Programs.

The TUSTEP format includes a reference number in front of every record; this machine
            reference has been calculated in such a way that it agrees with the textual reference.
            In the ASCII--format of the input file this machine reference is lost.

Some of the tools for textual analysis which can be produced from the input format have
            been published for the Brahmapurāṇa: Peter Schreiner, Renate Soehnen: Sanskrit Indices
            and Text of the Brahmapurāṇa. Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz, 1987.

The following list gives a survey of programs (German names in parentheses) developed
            for the processing of our input:

Any of the transliterated versions (i..e. ed. Johnston or ed. Cowell) can be
                  extracted (GRUNDTEXTKOP, VARTEXTKOP)

The machine references in TUSTEP are calculated from the references in the text
                  (REFRECHNEN).

The text format (i..e. the conventionally transliterated text without markers;
                  with compounds and sandhis reconstituted) can be generated (TEXTFORM). This
                  version can be processed for output in Devanāgarī with programs which work on the
                  basis of transliterated input (e.g., TeX).

The pausa format of the text is generated by changing all the characters marked
                  by * or + according to the sandhi rules of Sanskrit grammar. Each word appears in
                  the phonetic form which it would assume at the end of a line (e.g., ādibhir*,
                  ādibhiṣ*, ādibhiś*, ādhibhis* all become ādibhiḥ). Members of compounds are
                  separated. (PAUSAFORM)
Indexes:
-- KWIC-Index (from modified input format)

-- Pāda-Index (from modified text format) -- wordforms (from pausa
                  format)
-- reverse index of wordforms (from pausa format)

All indexes are sorted according to the Devanāgarī alphabet and may include frequencies
            (absolute and relative) and formatting commands for the output.

Those interested in any version or output other than the transliterated input format
            with variants may contact:

Peter Schreiner, Indologisches Seminar, Universität Zürich, Rämistr. 68, CH--8001
            Zürich, Switzerland.

I would appreciate if those who in using this electronic text change it or add to it
            would inform me about their views and intentions and methods and results; those who use
            this text for their research while preparing a publication should feel morally obliged
            to send me an offprint. (I hope I am not asking too much!)

The text of the Johnston edition was transliterated on the basis of a cursory
               reading; the typed input was compared with the edition by Cowell, partly as a routine
               of proof--reading, partly in order to be able to add variant readings from the older
               edition. (The conventions for inputting variants are described below.) Proof--reading
               and insertion of variants was done "manually" and I (Peter Schreiner) do not
               guarantee completeness. The additional passages in Cowell at the beginning of the
               poem were not transliterated completely, and the additional chapters at the end were
               not transliterated at all.

The published edition from which this e-text was transcribed is printed in the
               Devanāgarī script. The electronic text below is in a lossless transliteration using
               the Latin alphabet. The transliteration scheme used is the IAST (
The International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration

). IAST differs in
               small ways from ISO 15919, but is preferred by most working Sanskrit scholars.
               Conversion of this file to ISO 15919 can be achieved by performing the following
               replacements throughout the file:
ṛ -> r̥ and ṃ -> ṁ

Annotations, remarks etc. by the editor of the transliteration are enclosed in
                  square brackets.

Annotations by the editor(s) of the edition which served as source of the
                  transliteration (e..g. conjectures, markers for lacunae etc.) which are part of
                  the printed edition are enclosed in pointed parentheses.

Colophons which are part of the printed edition are enclosed by double square
                  brackets.

content.value: Sandhi

The "principle of transliteration" has been that the input format should
                  reproduce the letters of the printed text as closely as possible, i.e., that one
                  types what one sees. However, markers are added (in the transliteration) to what
                  is printed (in Devanāgarī) to indicate that fact that a printed (and consequently
                  typed) letter has undergone some sandhi change.

A sandhi change is defined with regard to the "pausa form" of a word, i..e. the
                  form a word would take at the end of a line or out of context (vigraha). Note that
                  this pausa form need not be identical with the stem which would be entered in a
                  dictionary.

Thus, (final and initial) consonants which have undergone a sandhi change in the
                  text are marked by "*". Similarly, final vowels which have changed due to sandhi
                  are marked by "*" (e.g., "āsīd* rājā nalo* nāma").

In case of vowel sandhi the sandhi is dissolved and marked (e.g., na*asti,
                  ca*eva). Similarly, avagraha is reconstituted, the originally omitted initial "a"
                  being marked as sandhi vowel (e.g., devo* *api).

In some special cases the marking of sandhi has to be extended to include some
                  disambiguating information:

-- to half--vowels which substitute for a long vowel the diacritic for
                        "long vowel" (-) is added (e.g., devy-* api);

-- if final -ā in sandhi does not stand for -āḥ (with visarga), then the
                        original vowel which has been substituted by the -ā is added (e.g., lokae*
                        eva, where "loka eva" is printed, which is the sandhi form for "loke
                        eva").

In case of "double sandhi" the sandhi is marked by double "**", e.g., sa**eva in
                  case of "saiva" instead of "sa* eva").

Blank is inserted between words wherever this is possible in transliteration
                  (though not necessarily in Devanāgarī), e.g., "hy* api", "nalo* *api".
Compounds

Another feature which exceeds what might be expected from a straightforward
                  transliteration is the separation of nominal compounds. Separation of compounds is
                  marked by inserting + between the members of a compound (e.g., brahma+purāṇa,
                  buddha+carita). In case of sandhi, the + functions also as sa.mdhi--marker, i..e.
                  no additional sandhi--marker is added (e.g., tapo+vane, mahā+ātmanaḥ).

Separation of compounds is restricted to nominal compounds (including
                  upapāda--compounds like ura+ga, go+pī) and does not include grammatical analysis.
                  For details, special cases etc. see the introduction to Sanskrit Indices and Text
                  of the Brahmapurāṇa, Wiesbaden 1987, p. xvi--xvii, by P. Schreiner and R.
                  So"hnen.
Variae lectiones
Variants

The beginning of the passage for which a variant exists is marked by opening
                  parenthesis. In deciding about the extension of the text thus marked, the changes
                  generated for the text format had to be taken into consideration. This meant that
                  occasionally words which are identical in the base text and in the variant are
                  included in the parentheses, since in the text format (sa.mhita) the beginning of
                  a variant could not be printed if that word is joined to the preceding word in
                  vowel sandhi. Thus we write "... (mahā+ātmā Xmahā+puruṣaḥ) ...", even though the
                  "mahā+" is identical in both versions.

The beginning of the variant is marked by a siglum, viz. by a single capital
                  letter (capital letters are used exclusively for that purpose in the
                  transliteration). Several sigla are separated by a comma (no blank) -- which does
                  not occur in this file of course. There is no blank between the siglum and the
                  variant.

If there are several variants for the same passage of the base text, they are
                  listed sequentially. The variant (or the last variant if there is more than one)
                  is closed by the closing parenthesis. The blank before the next word is considered
                  to belong to the variant and is put inside the parentheses. The continuation of
                  the base text follows without intermediate blank.
Schematic pattern:
Interpolations

Interpolations are treated as "variants without base text", i..e. siglum follows
                  immediately upon the opening parenthesis. The siglum is repeated before the
                  closing parenthesis which marks the end of the interpolation. This allows for the
                  input of variants within interpolations which are attested in more than one
                  source.

Long interpolations may be entered as a sequence of separate interpolations (e.g.,
                  verse by verse). Interpolated lines are (may be) marked by "X" at the beginning of
                  the line (which is meant to mark "star"--passages as e.g., in the criticial
                  edition of the MBh).
Omissions

Passages from the base text which are omitted in any of the variant texts are
                  marked by double parentheses plus siglum enclosing the omitted passage (which may
                  also be individual words).

children.translated_text: First Canto. |1|
Bestowing transcendent glory, surpassing the Creator,
dispelling darkness, outshining the sun-bearer,
driving away the heat of summer, conquering the beautiful moon,

children.text: Xsa* vandyate *arhann* iha yasya na*upamā |1.1| C)
children.translated_text: he is worshipped here as an <s>Arhat</s> (worthy one), to whom there is no equal. |1.1|
There was, with the splendor of its broad and lofty ridges,
its flanks surrounded as if by rows of rain clouds,
its high-peaked pinnacles penetrating the sky,
the city of <s>Kapilavastu</s>, the dwelling of the great sage. |1.2|
As if having stolen the cloud-glory of Mount <s>Kailāsa</s> by its white and lofty conduct,

children.text: Xbhramād upetān vahad+ambu+vāhān |saṃbhāvanāṃ* vā sa+phalī+cakāra |1.3| C)
children.translated_text: it bore rain clouds that came out of confusion, or else it made worthy of honor. |1.3|
Where, amidst the radiance of jewels,
darkness found no room, just as poverty finds none,
and from the joy of dwelling with supremely excellent citizens,
royal splendor seemed to smile. |1.4|
In that beautiful grove, the queen,
observing the time of her delivery,
repaired to a couch covered with a canopy,
attended and celebrated by thousands of women. ||1.8|
Then the <s>Puṣya</s> star became bright,
and from the side of that queen, consecrated by vows,
a son was born for the welfare of the world,
without pain and without affliction. ||1.9|

children.text: Verse 1.9 corresponds to 1.25 in ed. Cowell.

children.translated_text: [lacuna]
Just as <s>Aurva</s> was born from the thigh, and <s>Pṛthu</s> from the hand,
and <s>Māndhātṛ</s>, equal to <s>Indra</s>, from the head,
and <s>Kakṣīvat</s> from the region of the arm and shoulder —
of such a kind was his birth. ||1.10|
Like the fierce sun rising from a morning cloud,
he too, emerging from his mother's womb,
with radiant rays that dispelled the darkness,
made the world gleam like gold. |1.26|
Then, seeing him just born, bright as a golden sacrificial post,
the thousand-eyed <s>Indra</s>, pleased, gently received him;
with showers of <s>Mandāra</s> flowers upon his head,

children.text: Xkhān* nir+male ca vinipetatur* ambu+dhāre |1.27| C)
children.translated_text: pure streams of water fell from the sky. |1.27|
Carried by the chief gods,
delighting them with the nets of his body's radiance,
he surpassed in beauty the new moon-king
stationed above the mesh of twilight clouds. |1.28|
Having gradually emerged from the womb,
he shone as if fallen from the sky, not born from a womb,
for one whose soul had been cultivated through many eons
was born in full consciousness, not in delusion. ||1.11|
He who shone with radiance, steadfastness, and glory,
like the young sun descended upon the earth —
though exceedingly brilliant, when gazed upon,
he captivated the eyes like the moon. ||1.12|
For he, with the blazing splendor of his own body,
dimmed the light of lamps like the sun,
and with his beautiful hue of the finest gold,
he illuminated all the directions. ||1.13|
Without confusion, upright, and risen high,
with broad, extended strides free from stumbling,
thus firm, he took seven steps,
like the constellation of the Seven Sages. ||1.14|
"I am born for enlightenment, for the welfare of the world;
this is my final birth" —
looking upon the four directions with a lion's gait,
he uttered these words that would bring about the ultimate purpose. ||1.15|
From the sky, two streams of water, bright as moonbeams,
one cool and one warm in potency,
for the bodily comfort of that supreme one,
fell upon his gentle head. ||1.16|
Upon a glorious canopied bed, with limbs gleaming like gold,
its feet of <s>vaidūrya</s> (beryl), as he lay reclining,
out of reverence, with golden lotuses in hand,
the lords of the <s>Yakṣas</s> stood surrounding him. ||1.17|
And the celestial beings in the sky, born of <s>Māyā</s>,
by the power of him before whom they bowed their heads,
held a white parasol over him
and chanted supreme blessings for his enlightenment. ||1.18|
The great <s>Nāgas</s> (serpent-kings), thirsting for the excellence of the <s>Dharma</s>,
who had served the <s>Buddhas</s> of the past,
fanned him with eyes distinguished by devotion
and showered him with <s>Mandāra</s> flowers. ||1.19|
Pleased by the virtue of a <s>Tathāgata</s>'s arising,
the gods of pure abodes, of purified essence,
rejoiced, though free from passion,
for the welfare of the world immersed in suffering. ||1.20|
At his birth, the earth, anchored by the king of mountains,
trembled like a ship struck by the wind,
and a rain, laden with sandalwood, <s>utpala</s> lotuses, and <s>padma</s> lotuses,
fell from the cloudless sky. ||1.21|
Breezes blew, delightful and pleasing to the touch,
causing divine garments to fall;
the sun shone with even greater brilliance,
and fire, unkindle, blazed with a gentle flame. ||1.22|
In the northeastern quarter of the dwelling,
a well spontaneously appeared with clear water,
and the women of the inner apartments, struck with wonder,
performed rites there as at a sacred <s>tīrtha</s> (pilgrimage site). ||1.23|
By hosts of divine beings seeking the <s>Dharma</s>,
the grove was filled for the purpose of seeing him,
and even at the feet of the trees,
flowers blossomed unseasonably, along with fragrant offerings. ||1.24|

That which the royal science — neither <s>Bhṛgu</s> nor <s>Aṅgiras</s>,
those two dynasty-founding sages, composed;
the sons of those two, O gentle one, created that
in due time — <s>Śukra</s> and <s>Bṛhaspati</s>. ||1.41|
<s>Sārasvata</s> too proclaimed the lost

children.text: vedaṃ* punar* yaṃ* dadṛśur* na pūrve |
children.translated_text: <s>Veda</s>, which the ancients had never seen;
and <s>Vyāsa</s> likewise divided it into many parts,
which <s>Vasiṣṭha</s> had not done, being unable. ||1.42|
<s>Vālmīki</s> first composed poetry
which the great sage <s>Cyavana</s> had not composed;
and the medical science that <s>Atri</s> did not create
was later declared by the sage <s>Ātreya</s>. ||1.43|

children.translated_text: And the twice-born status that <s>Kuśika</s> did not attain,
the son of <s>Gādhin</s> obtained, O King;
<s>Sagara</s> set a boundary for the ocean
which the <s>Ikṣvākus</s> had not first established. ||1.44|
The mastery of the discipline of <s>Yoga</s> among the twice-born,
which others had not attained, <s>Janaka</s> achieved;
and the famous deeds of <s>Śauri</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) —
<s>Śūra</s> and his predecessors were powerless in those. ||1.45|

children.text: tasmāt pramāṇaṃ* na vayo* na (vaṃśaḥ Ckālaḥ )|
children.translated_text: Therefore, neither age nor lineage is the measure;
anyone anywhere may attain preeminence in the world;
for, of kings and sages alike,
those deeds were accomplished by sons that were not accomplished by forefathers." ||1.46|
Thus the king, by those trusted <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>,
was both reassured and congratulated,
and he cast off the unwelcome doubt from his mind
and rose to even greater delight. ||1.47|
And, pleased, to those best of <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>,
he gave wealth preceded by honors, thinking:
"May this prince become a sovereign as declared,
and may he retire to the forests upon reaching old age." ||1.48|
Then, having learned of that birth as the one ending all births,
by means of omens and by the power of his austerities,
the great sage <s>Asita</s> came to the dwelling
of the lord of the <s>Śākyas</s>, out of thirst for the true <s>Dharma</s>. ||1.49|
Him, a knower of <s>Brahman</s>, radiant among the knowers of <s>Brahman</s>,
shining with the glory of <s>Brahman</s> and with the glory of austerity —
the king's preceptor ushered into the royal palace
with due respect and honor. ||1.50|
He entered the vicinity of the royal inner apartments,
with the rush of joy occasioned by the prince's birth,
composed, as if entering a forest (with the familiarity of a forest),
by the eminence of his austerity and the shelter of his old age. ||1.51|
Then the king, having properly honored that sage seated
with the offering of water for the feet and the welcome-offering,
invited him with due hospitality,
as <s>Antideva</s> once invited <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>. ||1.52|
"I am blessed, and this family of mine is worthy of favor,
since the Blessed One has come to see me.
Command what I should do, O gentle one;
I am your disciple — you should trust me," he said. ||1.53|
Thus invited by the king,
the sage, with his whole being, fittingly,
with eyes wide with wonder,
spoke words deep and composed: ||1.54|
"This is fitting for you, O great-souled one,
who welcome guests, who are generous, who love the <s>Dharma</s>;
befitting your character, lineage, wisdom, and age,

children.translated_text: that your kind regard should be thus toward me. ||1.55|

children.translated_text: having acquired wealth through subtle <s>Dharma</s>,
always giving it away according to rite, became
rich in austerities though poor in possessions. ||1.56|
But as for the purpose of my coming —

children.text: tan* me śṛṇu prītim upehi ca tvam |
children.translated_text: hear it and be glad:
I heard a divine voice on the path of the sun saying,
'Your son is born for enlightenment.' ||1.57|

children.text: śrutvā vacas* tac* ca manaś* ca yuktvā |
children.translated_text: Having heard that utterance and applied my mind,
and having known by omens, I have come here,
out of desire to see the banner of the <s>Śākya</s> clan,
raised aloft like the banner of <s>Śakra</s> (Indra)." ||1.58|
Having heard this speech,
the king, his gait quickened by joy and agitation,
taking the prince who was in the lap of the nurse,
showed him to that one rich in austerity. ||1.59|
Then the great sage beheld the prince
with wheel-marks on his feet, webbed fingers and toes,
with the <s>ūrṇā</s> (tuft of hair between the brows), and concealed organs like an elephant —
he gazed at him with wonder. ||1.60|
And beholding him lying in the nurse's lap,
like the son of <s>Agni</s> (Fire) lying in the lap of the goddess,
tears trembled at the edges of his eyelashes,
and he sighed and turned his face upward toward heaven. ||1.61|
But the king, seeing <s>Asita</s> with eyes flooded with tears,
trembled with love for his son,
and with voice choked, his throat hoarse with suppressed tears,
he asked with joined palms and bowed body: ||1.62|
"His body differs but little from the gods,
his birth is wondrously radiant,
and you declare his future destiny to be supreme —

children.text: taṃ* prekṣya kasmāt tava dhīra bāṣpaḥ ||1.63|
children.translated_text: then why, O steadfast one, your tears upon seeing him? ||1.63|
"Is the prince long-lived, O Blessed One?
Surely he is not born for my grief?
The handful of water I have somehow obtained —

children.text: na khalv* imaṃ* pātum upaiti kālaḥ ||1.64|
children.translated_text: surely time does not come to drink it up? ||1.64|
Is he the imperishable treasure-house of my fame?
Is the essential gem of my dynasty secure?
Shall I depart happily to the next world,
an unblinking, single eye even while my son sleeps? ||1.65|

children.text: kac+cin* na me jātam a+phullam eva |
children.translated_text: Has not the shoot of my family, not yet blossomed,
become a share of withering?

children.text: kṣipraṃ* vibho brūhi na me *asti śāntiḥ |
children.translated_text: Tell me quickly, O mighty one, for I have no peace;
you know the affection of kinsmen for a son."
Then, perceiving the king's agitation arising from the thought of something undesirable,
the sage spoke to the lord of men:

children.text: mā bhūn* matis* te nṛ+pa kā+cid* |
children.translated_text: "Let not your mind, O King, be directed

children.text: anyā niḥ+saṃśayaṃ* tad* yad* avocam asmi ||1.67|
children.translated_text: elsewhere—what I have said is without doubt.
There is no change in me regarding this one;
but I am troubled regarding my own disappointment,

children.text: kālo* hi me yātum ayaṃ* ca jāto* |
children.translated_text: for the time has come for me to depart, and this one has been born—
he who shall know the destruction of birth, so difficult to attain.
Having abandoned the kingdom, indifferent to sense-objects,
through fierce efforts attaining the truth,
he shall blaze forth in the world to destroy the darkness of delusion,
for he is a sun made of knowledge.
From the ocean of suffering, with the foam of disease scattered about,
with the waves of old age, with the fierce current of death—
this one shall carry across the world that is being carried away,
afflicted, by the great vessel of knowledge.
The river of <s>Dharma</s>, whose current is the force of wisdom, whose embankment is steadfast moral conduct,
cool with <s>samādhi</s> (meditative concentration), whose water-birds are the wheel of vows—
this supreme river set flowing by him,
the living world, tormented by thirst, shall drink.
To those afflicted by suffering, enveloped by sense-objects,
standing on the path through the wilderness of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
he shall proclaim the path of liberation,
as if to travelers who have lost their way.
To the people of the world being burned
by the fire of passion fueled by sense-objects,
he shall bring relief through the rain of <s>Dharma</s>,
like a great cloud raining at the end of scorching heat.
The door whose bolt is craving and whose panel is the darkness of delusion,
the door for the departure of beings—
this one shall shatter with the supreme
blow of the true <s>Dharma</s>, so hard to approach.
Of the world, bound by its own nooses of delusion,
overcome by suffering, without refuge—
having awakened, this king of <s>Dharma</s>
shall bring about liberation from bondage.

children.text: tan* mā kṛthāḥ śokam imaṃ* prati tvam |
children.translated_text: Therefore do not grieve regarding this one;

children.text: (asmin sa* śocyo* *asti Ctat saumya śocye hi )manuṣya+loke |
children.translated_text: he who is to be grieved for in this human world
is the one who, whether through delusion, the pleasures of desire, or through pride,
will not hear his ultimate <s>Dharma</s>.

children.text: bhraṣṭasya tasmāc* ca guṇād* ato* me |
children.translated_text: And having fallen from that virtue, for me
though I have attained the <s>dhyānas</s> (meditations), there is only unfulfilled purpose;
for, deprived of hearing that <s>Dharma</s>,
I consider even a dwelling in heaven a misfortune."
Having heard the meaning, the lord of men, together with his friends and wife,
abandoning sorrow, rejoiced,
thinking, "Such is this son of mine!"

children.text: mene sa* hi svām api (sāravattām Csāramattām )||1.78|
children.translated_text: For he considered even himself to be of great worth.
But that he would go by the path of the sages—
this made his heart subject to anxiety;
not indeed that he was not one who favored <s>Dharma</s>,
but he foresaw danger from the destruction of his lineage.
Then the sage <s>Asita</s>, having disclosed the truth
about the son to the king anxious about his son,
being gazed upon with great respect,
departed by the path of the wind, just as he had come.
Having fulfilled his purpose and having seen the son of his sister's son,
and having heard the sage's words and being of the same conviction,
that virtuous one, with compassion in many ways,
made arrangements as if for his own dear son.
The king too, delighted at the birth of his son,
releasing the bonds pertaining to sense-objects,
performed, as was proper for the family,
the birth-rites for his dear son.
When ten days had passed,
with purified mind, surrounded by supreme joy,
he performed the recitations, oblations, auspicious rites, and
worship of deities for the supreme well-being of his son.
And also, cows numbering a full hundred thousand,
with firm and strong calves, with gold-tipped horns,
not yet old, yielding milk—
he himself gave to the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> for the prosperity of his son.
Then, the self-controlled one, having performed
rites of manifold kinds that gratified his own heart,
at an auspicious, fortunate moment, on a day of good qualities,
joyfully set his mind on the entry into the city.
Then, a palanquin of great value, made of elephant ivory,
bearing white and white flowers, adorned with jeweled lamps—
the queen, now a mother, ascended for good fortune,
having bowed to the deities.
Then, having caused his wife to enter the city first,
attended by elders, with her child as her lord,
the king too went, accompanied by throngs of citizens,
like <s>Maghavān</s> (<s>Indra</s>) being worshipped by the immortals going to heaven.
Then, the <s>Śākya</s> king, entering his palace,
delighted as <s>Bhava</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) at the birth of <s>Ṣaṇmukha</s> (<s>Kārttikeya</s>),
with a face full of joy, saying 'this and this,'
distributed gifts that bestowed manifold nourishment and fame.
Thus, by the prosperity of the birth of the king's son,
that city called <s>Kapila</s> (<s>Kapilavastu</s>), together with its countryside,
like the city of <s>Dhanada</s> (<s>Kubera</s>) strewn with <s>Apsarases</s>,
became joyful, as at the birth of <s>Nalakūbara</s>.
Thus ends the first canto, named 'The Birth of the Blessed One,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>.
Second Canto.
From the birth of that one destined to end birth and old age,
that self-born king, conqueror of self—
day by day, through wealth, elephants, horses, and allies,
he grew, like a river through the force of its waters.
Of this and that wealth and jewels,
of gold both wrought and unwrought—

children.text: tadā hi (na*ekān sa* nidhīn avāpa Cna*eka+ātma+nidhīn avāpi )|
children.translated_text: at that time he obtained not one but many treasures,
exceeding even the burden of wishes.
And those Himalayan elephants, proud with rut,
whom even with lotus-like bull-elephants one could not lead into the circle—
they, fierce with intoxication,
attended upon him without any effort.
With horses of various brand-marks, with fresh golden trappings,
adorned, with flowing manes, and others too,
his city was stirred,
obtained through strength, friendship, and wealth.
Well-nourished and contented in his kingdom,
virtuous, free from impurity, of excellent milk—
there were many cows, with thriving calves,
yielding abundant milk.
His enemy attained neutrality;
the neutral one turned to friendship;
his friend especially grew in firmness;

children.text: dvāv* asya pakṣāv* a+paras tu (na*āsa Cnāśam )||2.6|
children.translated_text: he had two parties, but not an adversary.
Likewise, with the sound of gentle breezes and clouds,
with lightning-earrings adorning the clouds,
without the fault of hailstorms and thunderbolts,
the sky rained at the right time and place.
The crops grew fruitfully, according to the season,
even without the labor of plowing being performed;
and those very herbs
became exceedingly rich in essence and in substance.
Even at the time that causes anxiety about the body,
when the pressure of labor comes, as in a battle—
healthy, in comfort, and free from illness,
women gave birth according to the natural course of time.
Even when wealth was obtainable from others through different means,
men did not seek from others;
and even a noble man solicited, though of slender means,
none at that time turned away.
There was no one disrespectful to kinsmen, nor one who did not give,
nor one without vows, nor a liar, nor one causing harm;
there was no such person in his kingdom,
as in the kingdom of King <s>Yayāti</s>, son of <s>Nahuṣa</s>.
For gardens, temples, and hermitages,
for wells, drinking-halls, ponds, and groves—
the lovers of <s>Dharma</s> performed rites there,
as if perceiving heaven before their very eyes.
Freed from famine, fear, and disease,
the people, delighted, took pleasure as if in heaven;

children.text: patnīṃ* patir* vā mahiṣī patiṃ* vā |
children.translated_text: wife did not transgress against husband,
nor husband against wife.
None pursued desire merely for pleasure;
none guarded wealth merely for the sake of desire;
none practiced <s>Dharma</s> merely for the sake of wealth;
none committed violence for the sake of <s>Dharma</s>.
Free from theft and the like, and from enemies,
his own domain was secure, freed from foreign powers—
safe and prosperous
was his kingdom, as in the ancient forest-free realm.
For at that time, at the birth of the king's son,
as in the kingdom of <s>Manu</s>, son of the sun,
joy prevailed, sin perished,
<s>Dharma</s> blazed forth, and corruption subsided.
Since such prosperity of the royal family
and the accomplishment of all goals came about,
therefore the king gave his son the name:
'This one is <s>Sarvārthasiddha</s> (Accomplisher of All Goals).'
But Queen <s>Māyā</s>, having seen the vast power of her son,
like a divine sage,
was unable to bear the joy that had arisen,
and therefore departed to heaven, as to an abode.
Then, the prince, like a divine child,
without distinction in affection and disposition—
his maternal aunt, of power equal to his mother,
raised him, growing as if of her own nature.
Then, like the young sun standing at the point of rising,
like a fire fanned by the wind,
the prince grew gradually and properly,
like the lord of the stars in the bright fortnight.
Then, from the houses of his well-wishers,
costly sandalwoods, strings of jewels, along with herbs in their covers,
and golden toy-chariots drawn by deer—
these were brought to him.
Ornaments suited to his age,
and golden toy elephants, deer, and horses,
and chariots yoked with toy oxen,
and dolls made of gold and silver, variously adorned.
Thus, attended upon with those various ministrations of sense-pleasure,
suited to his age,
though a child, he appeared as one who was not a child,

children.text: dhṛtyā ca śaucena dhiyā śriyā ca ||2.23|
children.translated_text: in steadfastness, purity, intelligence, and splendor.
Having properly passed through childhood

children.text: saṃprāpya (kāle pratipatti+karma Cbālaḥ sa* hi rāja+sūnuḥ )|
children.translated_text: and reached the age for the ritual of initiation—
in a few days he grasped the sciences
befitting his family, which would have taken many years.
But the king, having heard beforehand from the great sage <s>Asita</s>
about the future goal of supreme good for his son,
sought to engender in him attachment to sensual pleasures,

children.text: (vanāni yāyād* iti śākya+rājaḥ Cvṛddhir* bhavac+chākya+kulasya rājñaḥ )||2.25|
children.translated_text: the <s>Śākya</s> king (feared) he would go to the forests; (yet) there was growth for the royal family of the <s>Śākya</s> king. ||2.25|
Then from a family endowed with firm virtue,
a virtuous woman, possessed of beauty, modesty, and good conduct,
named <s>Yaśodharā</s>, of far-reaching fame,
he summoned as a wife, whose name matched her splendor. ||2.26|
Then, shining with surpassing beauty, this beloved of the lord of the earth,
the prince, resembling <s>Sanatkumāra</s>,
together with that bride of the <s>Śākya</s> lord,
sported like <s>Indra</s> of the thousand eyes with <s>Śacī</s>. ||2.27|
"How shall he not see anything that is disagreeable,
disturbing to the mind?" — thus reflecting,
the king assigned him a dwelling
within the upper chambers of palaces, not on the open ground. ||2.28|
Then, in palaces as white as autumn clouds,
adorned like celestial mansions on earth,
offering comfort in every season,
he sported with the splendid music of women. ||2.29|
With sweet tones from drums bound with gold girdles,
struck by the fingertips of women,
and with dances rivaling the dances of the finest <s>Apsarases</s>,
that palace shone like <s>Kailāsa</s>. ||2.30|
With melodious words and charming gestures,
with intoxicating, playful, and sweet laughter,
the women there delighted him,
with half-glances and arching brows. ||2.31|
Then, held by women skilled in the arts of love,
fierce in passion,
he did not descend from the palace roof to the earth,
like one of meritorious deeds not descending from a celestial mansion. ||2.32|
The king, however, for the sake of his very prosperity,
and urged by what was destined to be,
delighted in tranquility, ceased from evil,
embraced self-control, and shared with the virtuous. ||2.33|
He did not cling to the pleasures of desire like one unsteady,
nor did he take delight in what was unjust toward his subjects;
with firmness he conquered the restive steeds of the senses,

children.text: bandhūṃś* ca paurāṃś* ca guṇair* jigāya ||2.34|
children.translated_text: and surpassed his kinsmen and citizens with his virtues. ||2.34|
He did not study knowledge for the suffering of others;

children.text: jñānaṃ* śivaṃ* yat tu tad* adhyagīṣṭa |
children.translated_text: the knowledge that was auspicious—that he studied.
Just as for his own subjects,
so too for all beings he wished what is auspicious. ||2.35|
The brilliant star <s>Agni</s>, presiding deity of <s>Aṅgiras</s>,
he duly worshipped for the sake of his son's long life;
he offered oblations in the well-fed fire,

children.text: dadau dvi+jebhyaḥ kṛśanaṃ* ca gāś* ca ||2.36|
children.translated_text: and gave gold and cows to the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>. ||2.36|
He bathed his body to purify his mind as well,
with the waters of sacred fords and with the waters of virtue;
he drank the <s>Soma</s> prescribed by the <s>Vedas</s>, and also
the <s>Soma</s> born of the self—the deep joy of peace. ||2.37|

children.text: sāntvaṃ* babhāṣe na ca na*arthavad* yaj* |
children.translated_text: He spoke gently, and nothing that was without purpose;

children.text: jajalpa tattvaṃ* na ca vi+priyaṃ* yat |
children.translated_text: he uttered truth, and nothing that was displeasing;

children.text: sāntvaṃ* hy* a+tattvaṃ* paruṣaṃ* ca tattvaṃ* |
children.translated_text: for gentle words that are untrue, and harsh words that are true—
out of modesty he could not bring himself to utter even in his own heart. ||2.38|
In matters both agreeable and disagreeable that required action,
he did not fall into the sway of passion or aversion;
he cultivated what was auspicious and pure in conduct,

children.text: yajñaṃ* hi mene na tathā (yathā tat Cyathāvat )||2.39|
children.translated_text: for he did not value ritual sacrifice as much as that. ||2.39|
To a suppliant who came with hope, he immediately
cut short his thirst with streams of what should be given;
and without battle, by the whirling of his axe,
he shattered the swollen pride of enemies. ||2.40|
He punished one (vice), guarded seven (elements of the state),
abandoned seven (vices) also, and protected five (sources of revenue);
he attained the triple group (dharma, artha, kāma) and comprehended the triple group (of allies),
knew the two groups (of agreement and disagreement), and abandoned the two groups (of faults). ||2.41|
Even those who had committed offenses and deserved execution,
he neither slew nor looked upon with anger;
he bound them with gentleness and with just reward,
for even their banishment was regarded as leading to no harm. ||2.42|
He practiced the supreme vows of the <s>Ṛṣis</s>,
and dissolved enmities long accumulated;
he gathered renown fragrant with the perfume of virtue,
and swept away the stains that defile. ||2.43|
He did not wish to collect tribute not properly due,
nor did he wish to covet the possessions of others,
nor did he wish to speak unrighteously even to enemies,
nor did he wish to harbor anger in his heart. ||2.44|
While the lord of the earth conducted himself thus,

children.text: bhṛtyāś* ca paurāś* ca tathā*eva ceruḥ |
children.translated_text: his servants and citizens conducted themselves likewise,
as the senses of one whose mind is serene and tranquil
follow one who is devoted to <s>yoga</s>. ||2.45|
Then, in time, in <s>Yaśodharā</s> of lovely breasts,
bearer of his fair renown,
to the son of <s>Śuddhodana</s>, a son was born, rival of <s>Rāhu</s> in countenance,
<s>Rāhula</s> by name. ||2.46|
Then, having obtained the desired son, deeply gratified,
the king, regarding the growth of the family,
just as he had rejoiced at the birth of his son,
so too he rejoiced at the birth of his grandson. ||2.47|
"May my son's love for his son be just as mine for him"—
thus, joy arising in him,

children.text: kāle sa* taṃ* taṃ* vidhim ālalambe |
children.translated_text: at each proper time he undertook the due observances,
loving his son, as if desiring to ascend to heaven. ||2.48|
Standing on the path of the first royal sages
who were endowed with renown,
without abandoning the white vestments, he performed austerities,
and sacrificed with sacrifices free from animal slaughter. ||2.49|
Then that one of meritorious deeds blazed forth
with the splendor of kingship and the splendor of austerity;
illuminated by lineage, conduct, and wisdom,
like the thousand-rayed sun about to pour forth its radiance. ||2.50|
Having worshipped the hymn of <s>Svāyambhuva</s>,
the one of steadfast glory chanted for the stability of his son;
and he performed difficult deeds,
like <s>Prajāpati</s> at the beginning of creation, desiring to create beings. ||2.51|
He abandoned the sword and studied the scriptures;
he cultivated tranquility and endured self-restraint;
self-controlled, he did not indulge in any sense-object,
yet like a father he surveyed all the domains. ||2.52|
He bore the kingdom for the sake of his son,
his son for the sake of the family, and the family for renown;
renown for heaven, heaven for the sake of the self,
and the stability of the self he desired for the sake of <s>Dharma</s>. ||2.53|
Thus he performed <s>Dharma</s> of many kinds,
established among the good and confirmed by scripture,
thinking, "Having seen my grandson's face, how shall my son
not go to the forest?"—thus seeking reassurance. ||2.54|
Kings on earth who wish to preserve their own abiding glory
protect their sons;
but that lord of men, desiring <s>Dharma</s>,
guarded his son from <s>Dharma</s>, releasing him among sense-pleasures. ||2.55|
But all <s>Bodhisattvas</s> of incomparable nature,
knowing the taste of sense-pleasure, went to the forest after sons were born;
therefore, though the root cause had grown through accumulated deeds,

children.text: sa* ratim upasiṣeve bodhim (āpan* na yāvat Cāpanna+yāvat )||2.56|
children.translated_text: he continued to enjoy pleasure until he attained <s>Bodhi</s>. ||2.56|
Thus ends the second canto, named 'Life in the Inner Apartments,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |2|
Third Canto |3|
Then, one day, the groves with their soft green lawns,
resonating with the calls of male cuckoos at every step,
adorned with lotus pools,
and bound by songs—he heard of these forests. ||3.1|
Then, hearing of the delightful nature
of the city gardens, beloved of the womenfolk,
he formed the intention to go out,
like an elephant confined within a house. ||3.2|
Then the king, learning of the intention
of his son—of that wish of the mind—
fitting for his affection, his prosperity, and his youth,
commanded a pleasure-excursion. ||3.3|
And he had cleared from the royal road
any encounter with suffering common people,
thinking, "Let not the tender-hearted prince
become agitated in mind." ||3.4|
Those with missing limbs, with impaired senses,
the old, the sick, and the wretched in all directions,
they then removed with exceeding gentleness,
and made the royal road surpassingly beautiful. ||3.5|
Then, on the splendid royal road thus prepared,
the handsome prince with his well-trained attendants,
descending from the palace terrace at the proper time,
having received permission, went to the king. ||3.6|
Then the lord of men, tears coming to his eyes,
after smelling his son's head and gazing at him long,
said "Go!" with his voice,
but out of affection could not release him from his mind. ||3.7|
Then he mounted a golden chariot,
yoked with four calm horses
bearing ornaments of <s>Jāmbūnada</s> gold,
with bright, pure reins held by a skilled driver. ||3.8|
Then, on a road strewn with scattered, brilliant flower garlands,
with hanging wreaths and waving banners,
he proceeded with a fitting retinue,
like the moon with its stars through the sky. ||3.9|
With eyes widened by curiosity,
as if showered with half-open blue lotuses,
slowly, slowly he traversed the royal road,
being gazed upon from all sides by the citizens. ||3.10|
Some praised him for his gentle qualities,
others paid homage to his radiance;
some, seeing the splendor of his countenance,
wished him greatness and long life. ||3.11|
Hunchbacked women emerging from great houses,
and bands of dwarfs and <s>Kirāta</s> attendants,
and women from humble dwellings—
they all bowed like banners greeting a divine procession. ||3.12|
Then, hearing from the servant-folk the news
that the prince was indeed passing by,
women, desiring to see him, went to the palace terraces,
having received permission from the elders. ||3.13|
With their girdle-strings loosened and hanging,
with eyes still bewildered from being newly awakened,
with ornaments hastily put on,
restless with curiosity, they pressed around. ||3.14|
With the sounds of their feet on the palace stairs,
with the tinkling of girdles and the jingling of anklets,
startling the flocks of household birds,
and urging each other on in their haste, ||3.15|
some of these noble women,
though hurrying and eager,
were slowed in their gait by their wide
hips like chariots and their full breasts. ||3.16|
Another, though quite able to walk quickly,
restrained her pace and did not go swiftly,
out of modesty concealing, though she was bold,
the ornaments meant for private moments. ||3.17|
Of those women pressed together in mutual crowding,
their earrings jostled and shaken by the throng,
with their ornaments tinkling,
there was no rest at the windows. ||3.18|
But from those windows, the
with earrings placed by others' hands,
the lotus-faces of the women shone,
like lotuses clinging to the balconies. ||3.19|
Then, with the upper chambers thronged by young women,
their windows thrown open with curiosity,
the splendid city shone on all sides
like the sky with aerial palaces filled with <s>Apsarases</s>. ||3.20|
Because the windows were narrow,
with their earrings pressed against each other's cheeks,
the faces of the finest women shone
like clusters of bound lotuses. ||3.21|
Those women, gazing at the prince on the road,
seemed as if wishing to descend to the earth,
while the men, looking up at him with upturned faces,
seemed as if wishing to ascend to heaven. ||3.22|

children.text: dṛṣṭvā ca taṃ* rāja+sutaṃ* striyas* tā* |
children.translated_text: And seeing that prince, radiant
in body and in beauty,
those women softly said, 'Blessed is his wife' —
from the purity of their minds, and not from any other feeling. ||3.23|
This one, they say, with long and muscular arms,
like <s>Puṣpaketu</s> (Kāmadeva, the god of love) himself made visible in beauty,
will abandon royal glory and pursue the <s>Dharma</s> —
thus indeed they felt reverence toward him. ||3.24|
The prince, seeing the royal road thus filled
with citizens, modest, of pure and dignified appearance,
rejoiced somewhat at the sight of that first scene,
and felt as if he were experiencing a second birth. ||3.25|

children.text: puraṃ* tu tat svargam iva prahṛṣṭaṃ* |
children.translated_text: But seeing that city rejoicing like heaven,
the gods of pure abodes
created an old man to pass by,
for the purpose of stirring the son of the king. ||3.26|
Then the prince, seeing that man overcome by old age,
of a form different from other men,
addressed the charioteer with fixed and eager attention,
his gaze immovably fixed upon that very one: ||3.27|
"Who is this man approaching us, O charioteer,
with white hair, his hand clinging to a staff,
his eyes concealed by his brows, his body bent and loose —
is this some change in him, or his nature, or a chance occurrence?" ||3.28|
Thus addressed, the chariot-driver
revealed to the son of the king
this matter that should have been concealed — seeing no fault in it,
his mind bewildered by those very gods: ||3.29|
"The destroyer of beauty, the calamity of strength,
the source of grief, the ruin of pleasures,
the destroyer of memory, the enemy of the senses —
this is called old age, by which this man is broken. ||3.30|
He too drank his mother's milk in infancy,
in time he crawled upon the ground,
gradually becoming a handsome youth,
and by that same gradual process he has come to old age. ||3.31|

children.text: ity* evam ukte calitaḥ sa* kiṃ+cid* |
children.translated_text: When this was said, the prince was somewhat shaken
and spoke thus to the charioteer:
"Will this affliction come upon me too?"
To him, then, the charioteer replied: ||3.32|
"For your long-lived self too, this decline of age

Then he, whose understanding was pure from former dispositions,

Sighing deeply, shaking his head,

"Thus old age strikes without distinction —

even when witnessing such a thing before its very eyes. ||3.36|
Since this is so, O charioteer, turn back the horses;

For how can there be pleasure for me in a garden

"Is this affliction peculiar to him alone,

Hearing this, his mind was dejected,

and full of compassion,

"Seeing this affliction of disease among beings,

Having heard of the fear of disease, my mind

children.translated_text: And the king, seeing him return thus a second time,

And out of love, knowing his son's disposition,

Then the prince said to the charioteer:

Therefore, O charioteer, turn back our chariot;

children.translated_text: that is itself cause for alarm, since they too came to ruin. ||4.90|

children.text: māhātmyaṃ* na ca tan* manye |yatra sāmānyataḥ kṣayaḥ |
children.translated_text: Nor do I consider it true greatness where there is common destruction,
whether it be attachment to pleasures or discipline through self-mastery. ||4.91|
And as for what you said, that one should deal with women even through falsehood —
I cannot understand any falsehood, even if it be called courtesy. ||4.92|

children.text: na ca*anuvartanaṃ* tan* me |rucitaṃ* yatra na*ārjavam |
children.translated_text: Nor is that kind of compliance pleasing to me where there is no honesty;

children.text: sarva+bhāvena saṃparko* |yadi na*asti dhig* astu tat ||4.93|
children.translated_text: if there is no genuine connection with one's whole being, let it be cursed! ||4.93|
For one who is unsteady, who trusts in the false, who is attached and sees no fault —
what indeed should be deceived of a mind in which passion has arisen? ||4.94|
And if those inflamed with passion thus deceive each other,

children.text: nanu na*eva kṣamaṃ* draṣṭuṃ* |narāḥ strīṇāṃ* nṛṇām* striyaḥ ||4.95|
children.translated_text: then surely it is not fitting for men to behold women, nor women men! ||4.95|
Therefore, since things are thus, you should not seek to lead me astray —
me who am afflicted by suffering, who am subject to old age and death — into ignoble pleasures." ||4.96|
"Ah, how exceedingly steadfast and strong is your mind,
who sees substance in fleeting pleasures!
You cling to sensual objects even when the danger is extreme,
while watching beings on the road to death! ||4.97|
I, however, am timid and exceedingly anxious,
contemplating the peril of old age, calamity, and disease;

children.text: labhe na śāntiṃ* na dhṛtiṃ* kuto* ratiṃ* |
children.translated_text: I find neither peace, nor steadfastness, much less delight,
seeing the world blazing as if with fire. ||4.98|
Of a man who knows with certainty that death will come,
yet in whose heart passion arises —
I consider his consciousness to be made of iron,
for he neither fears nor weeps amid this great terror." ||4.99|
Then, as the prince delivered this discourse of resolute nature,
destructive of all dependence on desire,
the sun, whose disc delights the eyes of the people,
set behind the mountain. ||4.100|
Then, their ornaments and garlands worn in vain,
their arts of skill and tender advances having proved fruitless,
suppressing desire in their own hearts,
the women returned to the city, their hopes shattered. ||4.101|
Then, seeing the splendor of the people in the royal garden
again withdrawn at evening,
reflecting on the impermanence pervading all things,
the son of the earth's guardian entered his palace. ||4.102|

children.text: tataḥ śrutvā rājā viṣaya+vi+mukhaṃ* tasya tu mano* |
children.translated_text: Then the king, hearing that his son's mind was averse to pleasures,

children.text: na śiśye tāṃ* rātriṃ* hṛdaya+gata+śalyo* gaja* iva |
children.translated_text: did not sleep that night, like an elephant with a shaft lodged in its heart.
Weary from many and various counsel with his ministers,

children.text: na so* *anyat kāmebhyo* niyamanam apaśyat suta+mateḥ ||4.103|
children.translated_text: he could see no other restraint for his son's resolve than sensual pleasures. ||4.103|
Thus ends the fourth canto, named 'Thwarting by Women,' in the great poem <s>Śrī Buddhacarita</s>. |4|
Fifth Canto. |5|
He, the son of the <s>Śākya</s> king, thus tempted
even by the most supreme sensual pleasures,
attained neither firmness nor comfort,
like a lion gravely wounded by a poisoned arrow in the heart. ||5.1|
Then, one day, accompanied by suitable sons of ministers,
his friends who told wonderful stories,
desiring to see the forest land, longing for tranquility,
he set forth with the permission of the king. ||5.2|
Mounting his good steed <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s>,
with its new golden bridle jingling with little bells, its swaying yak-tail whisks and beautiful golden trappings,
he rode forth
like a standard of <s>Lotus</s> and <s>Tree</s> banners. ||5.3|
He went to a more remote tract of land at the forest's edge,

children.text: vana+lobhāc* ca yayau mahī+(guṇāc* ca Cguṇa+icchuḥ )|
children.translated_text: drawn by the charm of the forest and desirous of the earth's qualities,
and he beheld the earth being plowed,
its furrows resembling the ripples of water. ||5.4|
Its grass and stalks scattered by the plow,
strewn with tiny creatures, worms, and insects that had been killed —
beholding the earth in such a state,
he grieved intensely as if at the slaughter of his own kinsmen. ||5.5|
And seeing the men who were plowing,
their complexions altered by wind, sun, and dust,
and the draft oxen exhausted and distressed by the burden —
that supremely noble one felt the deepest compassion. ||5.6|
Then, dismounting from the horse's back,
he walked slowly upon the ground, overcome with sorrow,
reflecting on the arising and passing away of the world,

children.text: kṛpaṇaṃ* khalv* idam ity* uvāca (ca*ārtaḥ Cca*ārttaḥ )||5.7|
children.translated_text: and spoke in anguish: "Pitiable indeed is this!" ||5.7|
And desiring solitude of mind,
dismissing those friends who were his attendants,
beneath a beautiful, trembling-leaved tree,
he went to the solitary root of a rose-apple (<s>Jambū</s>) tree. ||5.8|
He sat down there on the ground, beautiful and pure,
with its turf gleaming like <s>vaidūrya</s> (beryl),
and reflecting on the arising and passing away of the world,
he grasped the path to steadiness of mind. ||5.9|
Having swiftly attained steadiness of mind,
freed from the afflictions beginning with the desire for sensual objects,
he attained the tranquil first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditative absorption),
which includes <s>vitarka</s> (initial thought) and <s>vicāra</s> (sustained thought) and is of the nature without outflows. ||5.10|
Then, having attained the <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) born of discrimination,
with its supreme delight and happiness,
he reflected further upon this:
having rightly perceived the course of the world with his mind — ||5.11|
"Pitiable indeed that a person, himself being
helplessly subject to the law of disease, old age, and destruction,
should feel disgust toward another who is stricken by age, ill, or dead,
being ignorant, blinded by intoxication! ||5.12|

children.text: iha ced* aham ī+dṛśaḥ svayaṃ san* |
children.translated_text: If I, being myself of such a nature,
were to feel disgust toward another of the same nature,

children.text: na bhavet sa+dṛśaṃ* hi tat kṣamaṃ* vā |
children.translated_text: it would not be fitting or proper
for one who knows this supreme truth. ||5.13|
Thus, as he rightly perceived
the faults of disease, old age, and calamity in the world,
the intoxication arising from strength, youth, and life
vanished from his mind in an instant." ||5.14|
He neither rejoiced nor grieved,
he felt no doubt, no sloth or drowsiness,
he took no delight in the qualities of desire,
nor did he hate or look down upon another. ||5.15|
Thus this understanding, dustless and pure,
grew in that great-souled one;
and unseen by other men,
a man in the guise of a mendicant (<s>bhikṣu</s>) approached him. ||5.16|
The son of the king asked him;
"Tell me who you are," and the other declared to him:
"O bull among men, fearing birth and death,
I am a wandering ascetic (<s>śramaṇa</s>), gone forth for the sake of liberation. ||5.17|
In this world subject to the law of decay, seeking release,
I seek that auspicious, imperishable state.
With equal regard for my own people and strangers,
I am free from the faults of passion toward sensual objects. ||5.18|
Dwelling here or there at the root of a tree,
in a deserted shrine, or on a mountain or in a forest,
I wander without possessions, without expectations,
accepting whatever alms come, for the sake of the supreme goal." ||5.19|
Thus, even as the prince looked on,
having spoken, he rose up into the sky;
for he was a celestial being who had come to that form to awaken the understanding
of another <s>Buddha</s>, for the sake of his mindfulness. ||5.20|
When he departed through the sky like a bird,
the prince was filled with joy and wonder,
and having thereby gained the concept of the <s>Dharma</s>,
he formed the resolve to go forth. ||5.21|
Then, equal to <s>Indra</s>, having conquered the horses of his senses,
desiring to enter the city, he mounted his supreme horse.
but looking back at his attendant people,
he did not enter the forest he desired.
He, desiring to bring about the destruction of old age and death,
having fixed his mind on forest-dwelling while remaining mindful,
entered the city again, not out of desire,
like a lord of elephants returning to the enclosure from the forest grounds.
"Happy indeed and content is that woman

children.text: patir* ī+(dṛkṣa* iha*āyata+akṣa Cdṛk tvam iva*āyata+akṣa )yasyāḥ |
children.translated_text: whose husband is such as this one, O long-eyed one!"
Thus a princess, seeing him
entering on the road, spoke with palms joined.
Then he, whose voice was like a great thundercloud,
heard this utterance and attained supreme peace;
for having heard the word <s>nirvṛtā</s> (content/extinguished),
he set his mind on the method of <s>Parinirvāṇa</s> (complete cessation).
Then, he whose stature was like the peak of a golden mountain,
whose arms resounded like an elephant-cloud-bull,
who had arisen passion for the imperishable <s>Dharma</s> against decay,
whose valor was like a moon-faced lion, entered the palace.
Then, walking with the gait of a lion-king, he approached
the king, who was being attended by groups of ministers,
blazing like <s>Maghavān</s> (<s>Indra</s>) in the assembly of the <s>Maruts</s>—
like <s>Sanatkumāra</s> in the triple heaven.
Having prostrated and spoken with palms joined:
"Grant me, O lord of men, gracious permission;
I wish to go forth as a renunciant for the sake of liberation,
for the separation of this people is certain."
Hearing these words, the king
trembled like a tree struck by an elephant;
grasping his lotus-like joined palms,
he spoke these words, his throat choked with tears:
"Withdraw this intention, my son,
for it is not the time for you to resort to <s>Dharma</s>;
in the first period of life, when the mind is unsteady,
they say the practice of <s>Dharma</s> is full of faults.
For one whose senses are curious about sense-objects,
whose resolve is unable to endure the hardships of vows—
the mind of a youth wavers from the forest,
especially one unacquainted with solitude.
But for me, O lover of <s>Dharma</s>, it is the time for <s>Dharma</s>,
having entrusted to you the royal splendor, you who are fit to bear it;
O one of firm valor, <s>Dharma</s> practiced with valor is fitting,

children.text: tava hitvā tu guruṃ* bhaved* a+dharmaḥ ||5.32|
children.translated_text: but to abandon one's elder—that would be <s>adharma</s>.
Therefore abandon this resolve;
for now, be devoted to the <s>Dharma</s> of a householder.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of youth—
for entering the ascetic grove is delightful only after that."
Hearing these words of the king,
he of the voice like a <s>kalaviṅka</s> (Indian cuckoo) bird replied:
"If you become my guarantor in four things, O King,
I shall not resort to the ascetic grove.
Let not my life be subject to death;

children.text: viharet svāsthyam idam ca me na rogaḥ |
children.translated_text: let this health of mine not be disturbed by disease;

children.text: na ca yauvanam ākṣipej* jarā me |
children.translated_text: let not old age assail my youth;
and let not misfortune carry away this prosperity."
To the son who had spoken of this difficult-to-obtain goal,
the <s>Śākya</s> king spoke these words:
"Abandon this thought, which has gone too far;
and an extravagant wish is laughable."
Then he, weighty as Mount <s>Meru</s>, spoke to his elder:
"If this course is not possible, I am not to be restrained;
for it is not fitting to hold back one who is being burned,
desiring to escape from a blazing house.
Since separation from the world is certain,

children.text: (nanu Cna tu )dharmāya varaṃ* (svayaṃ+viyogaḥ Ctv* ayaṃ* viyogaḥ )|
children.translated_text: is not voluntary separation better, for the sake of <s>Dharma</s>?
For surely death will forcibly separate me,
my purpose unfulfilled, my desires unsatisfied."
Having heard his son's resolve,
the son who desired liberation,
the lord of the earth, declaring 'He shall not go,'
arranged for guards and for the finest pleasures.
Then, instructed by the ministers as was proper,
with great respect and affection, according to the scriptures,
and restrained by his elder with falling tears,
he entered his dwelling, grieving.
By women with faces kissed by swinging earrings,
their breasts heaving with deep sighs,
with unsteady eyes—
he was gazed upon as if by fawn-like creatures.
For he, radiant as a mountain of gold,
who drove the hearts of noble women to ecstasy,
captivated their hearing, bodies, eyes, and very selves
through his speech, touch, form, and qualities.
When the day had passed, then to the upper palace,
blazing with his beauty like the sun,
desiring to destroy the darkness with his own radiance,
he ascended like the rising sun upon Mount <s>Meru</s>.
A candelabra blazing bright with gold,
its interior filled with the smoke of finest dark aloe incense—
ascending this, inlaid with diamond patterns,
he occupied the supreme golden seat.

children.text: tata* uttamam (uttama+aṅganās* taṃ* Cuttamāś* ca nāryo* )|
children.translated_text: Then the noblest women
attended upon him at night with music, as upon <s>Indra</s>,
like hosts of <s>Apsaras</s> attending upon the son of <s>Dravineśvara</s> (<s>Kubera</s>)
on the moon-white summit of the <s>Himavat</s>.
Yet even with those instruments rivaling divine music,

children.text: sa* tu tair* na*eva ratiṃ* yayau na harṣam |
children.translated_text: he experienced neither pleasure nor delight;
for that virtuous one, whose desire was for the happiness of the ultimate truth,
did not rejoice, since his longing was to go forth.
Then, by the gods of supreme austerity,
the <s>Akaniṣṭhas</s> (highest devas), having understood his resolve,
simultaneously sleep was brought upon the company of women,
and their bodily postures became distorted.
For one lay there sleeping
with her cheek resting on her unsteady hand,
having cast aside her beloved <s>vīṇā</s>, adorned with painted golden leaves,
which rested on her lap, as if in anger.
Another, sleeping with a flute grasped in her hand,
her white garment slipping from her breast,
appeared like a river whose lotuses are visited by lines of bees,
its banks laughing with water-foam.
With arms soft as the interior of a fresh lotus,
adorned with bracelets blazing with burnished gold,
another slept, embracing her arms
as if they were a lover, clasping a clay drum.
Others, adorned with ornaments of fresh gold,
wearing yellow garments of the finest kind,
fell helplessly in deep slumber,
like branches of a <s>karṇikāra</s> tree broken by an elephant.
Another, sleeping with her body-staff curved like a bow,
leaning against the side of a window,
shone with her beautiful necklace hanging down,
like a sculpted figure on a gateway panel.
The lotus-face of another, bent down,
its painted leaf-ornament bitten by her jeweled earring,
appeared like a hundred-petaled lotus with half-bent stalk,
struck by a sheldrake standing upon it.
Others, sleeping as if seated,
their bodies bending under the weight of their breasts,
embracing each other, shone
with arm-nooses wearing golden bracelets.
And one woman, embracing a large lute
as if it were a dear friend, slept,
rolling about, its beautiful golden string swaying,
her face disordered with the strap.
Another, with a small drum from the region of her arm and shoulder,
its beautiful cord slipped away,
as if having drawn down a beloved, exhausted from the end of amorous play,
between her thighs, she slept.
Others appeared with their eyes closed,
though they were large-eyed ones, with beautiful brows;
like lotus ponds with closed lotus buds
when the sun has set.
Another, with her loosened and disheveled hair,
the ends of her ornamental garments slipped from her hips,
lay with her necklace-strings scattered,
like a woman from a shrine toppled by an elephant.
Others, helpless, bereft of modesty,
though possessed of firmness, endowed with the qualities of beauty,
breathed heavily as they slept,
distorted, throwing their arms about, and yawned.
Others, their ornaments and garlands cast aside,
their garments loosened and unbound, unconscious,
with eyes white, unclosed, and motionless,
did not shine as they lay, resembling the dead.
With mouth-cavity agape, body spread out,
saliva dripping from the mouth, private parts exposed—
another lay as if intoxicated and rolling,
she did not speak; her distorted body swelled.
Thus the company of women, sleeping
in various postures befitting beings of their nature and lineage,
bore the appearance
of a lotus pond whose stalks are broken and tossed by the wind.
Having observed those young women lying thus,
distorted, their movements unsteady,
though possessed of beautiful bodies and sweet speech—
the prince became filled with disgust.
"Impure and distorted in the world of the living—
such is the nature of women;
but deceived by dress and ornaments,
man develops passion for the domain of women.
If a man were to examine the true nature of women,
and this kind of transformation in sleep—
surely he would not increase his heedlessness here;
but struck by the notion of their qualities, he goes to passion."
Thus, having discerned that opening,
the desire to go forth arose in him at night;
the gods, understanding his mind,
caused the door of the palace to be opened.
Then he descended from the roof of the palace,
reproaching those sleeping women,
and having descended, without hesitation
he passed through the first enclosure of the house.
Having awakened <s>Chandaka</s>, his swift
horse-attendant, he spoke thus:
"Bring the horse <s>Kanthaka</s> swiftly;
I wish to depart from here today to attain the deathless.

children.text: hṛdi yā mama tuṣṭir* adya jātā |
children.translated_text: The satisfaction that has arisen in my heart today,
and the resolve that is fixed in my mind—
even in a deserted place I feel as if I have a protector;
surely the desired goal is approaching me.

children.text: hriyam eva ca saṃnatiṃ* ca hitvā |
children.translated_text: Since the young women have cast aside modesty and decorum
and lie sleeping before me,
and since the door has opened by itself—
surely the time has come for me to depart from here today."
Then, receiving the command of his master,
though knowing the king's decree,
as if impelled in his mind by another,
he set his mind on bringing the horse.
Then, with mouth filled with a golden bit,
its back covered with a light saddle-blanket,
endowed with strength, spirit, speed, and noble lineage—
he brought that excellent horse to his master.
with extended loins, tail-root, and heels,
with short, delicate offspring, tail, and ears, well-composed,
with back, belly, and flanks curved and raised,
with broad nostrils, forehead, croup, and chest, ||5.73|
embracing that horse, broad-chested,
soothing it with a lotus-like hand,
he addressed it in a sweet, unfaltering voice,
as if desiring to enter the midst of an army: ||5.74|
"Many enemies, indeed, have been cast down
by the king mounted upon you in battle;
may I too, O best of horses, duly attain
the immortal state—therefore, exert yourself!" ||5.75|
"Companions in battle are easily found,
or in the enjoyment of pleasures, or in the acquisition of wealth;
but companions are hard to find for a man
who has fallen into misfortune or who seeks <s>Dharma</s>. ||5.76|
And those who are companions here
in tainted deeds or in the pursuit of <s>Dharma</s>—
as my inner self perceives,
those people are surely sharers of the same portion. ||5.77|
Therefore, knowing this to be righteous—
my departure from here for the welfare of the world—
O best of horses, with your speed and valor,
strive for your own welfare and the welfare of the world!" ||5.78|
Having thus instructed the noble horse like a friend
in the task, the best of men, desiring to go to the forest,
resplendent with the dark luster of his gait,
mounted the white horse like the sun mounting an autumn cloud. ||5.79|
Then that noble steed, avoiding the sharp sound of the night
that would awaken the attendants,
with restrained jaw and stilled neighing,
proceeded with steps freed as if startled. ||5.80|
Then <s>Yakṣas</s>, bowing their bodies,
with lotus-like hands adorned with golden bracelets on their wrists,
pushing aside the lotuses as it were,
held up his hooves with their fingertips, moving with startled steps. ||5.81|
The city gates, closed with heavy bars and door-panels,
which could not easily be opened even by elephants—
as the prince departed, those gates,
noiseless, of their own accord swung open. ||5.82|
Having made up his mind, indifferent, he left behind
his father devoted to him, his infant son,
the loving people, and unsurpassed glory,
and departed from his father's city. ||5.83|
Then he, with wide eyes like stainless lotuses,
looking back at the city, roared the lion's roar:
"Until I have seen the far shore of birth and death,
I shall not enter the city called <s>Kapila</s> again!" ||5.84|
Hearing this utterance of his,
the attendant hosts of <s>Kubera</s> (lord of wealth) rejoiced,
and the assemblies of gods, with delighted minds,
augured for him the fulfillment of his resolve. ||5.85|
Other celestial beings with bodies like sacrificial fire,
knowing his extremely difficult resolve,
created light on the frosty path,
like rays of the moon streaming through openings in the clouds. ||5.86|
That horse, like the green steed of <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>),
galloping as if urged on in spirit,
through the sky reddish and harsh with stars,
covered very many leagues. ||5.87|
Thus ends the fifth canto, named 'The Great Departure,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |5|

seeing it, he felt as if rested,

children.translated_text: but one both devoted and capable—such as you—is rare on earth. ||6.7|

But even one's own people mostly become strangers in adversity. ||6.9|
A son is maintained for the sake of the family; a father is served for the sake of support;
the world embraces out of expectation—there is no selfless affection without a cause. ||6.10|

children.text: kim uktvā bahu saṃkṣepāt |kṛtaṃ* me su+mahat priyam |
children.translated_text: Why say much? In brief, you have done me a very great kindness.
Now turn back, taking the horse—I have reached the wished-for destination." ||6.11|
Having spoken thus, that mighty-armed one, desiring to repay,

Taking from his diadem the blazing, luminous jewel,

children.text: bruvan vākyam idaṃ* tasthau |sa+āditya* iva mandaraḥ ||6.13|
children.translated_text: he stood, speaking these words, like Mount <s>Mandara</s> with the sun. ||6.13|
"With this jewel, O <s>Chanda</s>, bowing many times, the king
is to be informed, without reserve of confidence, for the allaying of his grief: ||6.14|
'I have entered the forest of austerities for the destruction of birth and death—
not indeed through thirst for heaven, nor from lack of love, nor from anger. ||6.15|

children.text: tad* evam abhiniṣkrāntaṃ* |na māṃ* śocitum arhasi |

children.translated_text: he should not grieve; for even a long union, in time, will cease to be. ||6.16|

children.translated_text: Since separation is certain, therefore my mind is set on <s>Mokṣa</s> (liberation);

'He should not grieve for me who have departed to abandon grief;
rather, those attached to desires—the causes of grief—are the ones to be pitied.' ||6.18|

children.text: ayaṃ* ca kila pūrveṣām |asmākaṃ* niścayaḥ sthiraḥ |
children.translated_text: 'And this, indeed, was the firm resolve of our ancestors;
therefore, walking on the path that is my inheritance, I am not to be grieved for.' ||6.19|
'There are heirs to wealth when a man's fortune turns,

children.translated_text: but heirs to <s>Dharma</s> on earth are rare, or do not exist.' ||6.20|

children.text: yad* api syād* a+samaye |yāto* vanam asāv* iti |
children.translated_text: 'And even if it be said that he has gone to the forest at an untimely age—
there is no wrong time for <s>Dharma</s> when life is flickering.' ||6.21|

children.text: tasmād* adya*eva me śreyaś* |cetavyam iti niścayaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'Therefore my resolve is that my welfare must be pursued this very day;

children.text: jīvite ko* hi viśrambho* |mṛtyau praty+arthini sthite ||6.22|
children.translated_text: for who can trust in life when death stands as an adversary?' ||6.22|
"With such words and more, O gentle one, the lord of the earth is to be informed;

children.text: prayatethās* tathā ca*eva |yathā māṃ* na smared* api ||6.23|
children.translated_text: and strive also so that he may not even think of me. ||6.23|
Moreover, you may speak to the king even of my faults;
through faults, affection is abandoned; and through the abandonment of affection, one does not grieve." ||6.24|
Hearing these words, <s>Chandaka</s>, distraught with grief,
replied in a voice choked with tears, with palms joined: ||6.25|
"By this intention of yours that brings anguish to your kinsmen,

children.text: bhartaḥ sīdati me ceto* |nadī+paṅkae* iva dvi+paḥ ||6.26|
children.translated_text: my heart, O master, sinks like an elephant in river mud. ||6.26|
Whose tears would not be aroused by this resolve of yours?
Even in a heart of iron—how much more in one distraught with love! ||6.27|
This delicacy, worthy of palace couches and mansions—here;
and there, the ground of the ascetics' grove, rough with <s>darbha</s>-grass shoots! ||6.28|

children.text: śrutvā tu vyavasāyaṃ* te |yad* aśvo* *ayaṃ* (mayā*āhṛtaḥ Cmayā hṛtaḥ )|
children.translated_text: But as for the horse brought here by me, upon hearing of your resolve—
O lord, I was compelled to do it by force—indeed, by fate alone. ||6.29|

children.text: kathaṃ* hy* ātma+vaśo* jānan |vyavasāyam imaṃ* tava |
children.translated_text: For how could I, being in control of myself, knowing this resolve of yours,
have brought forward the horse—the grief of <s>Kapilavastu</s>? ||6.30|
Therefore you ought not, O mighty-armed one, to abandon

children.text: snigdhaṃ* vṛddhaṃ* ca rājānaṃ* |sad+dharmam iva nāstikaḥ ||6.31|
children.translated_text: the aged king who longs for his son, who is tender—like an atheist abandoning the true <s>Dharma</s>. ||6.31|
That second mother too, wearied by the toil of raising you—
O prince, you ought not forget her, like an ingrate forgetting a good deed. ||6.32|
Your queen, virtuous, of praiseworthy family, devoted to her husband,

children.text: devīm arhasi na tyaktuṃ* |(klībaḥ Cklīvaḥ )prāptām iva śriyam ||6.33|
children.translated_text: with her young son—you ought not abandon her, like a coward abandoning prosperity attained. ||6.33|
Your praiseworthy son, young <s>Rāhula</s>, the best of those who bear fame and <s>Dharma</s>—
you ought not abandon the child, like a dissolute man abandoning the highest renown. ||6.34|

children.text: atha bandhuṃ* ca rājyaṃ* ca |tyaktum eva kṛtā matiḥ |
children.translated_text: But if your mind is made up to abandon kinsmen and kingdom,

children.text: māṃ* na*arhasi vibho tyaktuṃ* |tvat+pādau hi gatir* mama ||6.35|
children.translated_text: you ought not, O lord, abandon me—for your feet are my sole refuge. ||6.35|
I am not able to go to the city with my heart ablaze,
leaving you in the forest, like <s>Sumantra</s> leaving <s>Rāghava</s> (<s>Rāma</s>). ||6.36|

children.text: kiṃ* hi vakṣyati (māṃ* rājā Crājā māṃ* )|tvad+ṛte nagaraṃ* gatam |
children.translated_text: What indeed will the king say to me, come to the city without you?
And what, having proper regard, shall I say to your inner chambers? ||6.37|

children.text: yad* apy* āttha*api nairguṇyaṃ* |vācyaṃ* nara+patāv* iti |
children.translated_text: And as for what you say—that even my faults should be told to the king—

children.text: kiṃ* tad* vakṣyāmy* a+bhūtaṃ* te |nir+doṣasya muner* iva ||6.38|
children.translated_text: how shall I speak what is untrue of you, who are faultless like a sage? ||6.38|
With a heart full of shame, with a tongue that falters—

children.text: ahaṃ* yady+api vā brūyāṃ* |kas* tac* *chraddhātum arhati ||6.39|
children.translated_text: even if I were to speak, who would be worthy to believe it? ||6.39|
or would believe it—
He who would speak of the harshness of the moon,
he, O knower of faults, might speak of your faults and believe them. ||6.40|
For one always compassionate, one who is ever aware of others' sorrow—
abandoning the affectionate is not fitting. Turn back! Be gracious to me!" ||6.41|
Hearing the speech of <s>Chandaka</s>, overcome with grief,
the best of speakers replied calmly, with supreme steadfastness: ||6.42|
"Regarding my separation, O <s>Chanda</s>, let this grief be abandoned;
for diversity of states is inevitable among embodied beings born in different lives. ||6.43|

children.text: sva+janaṃ* yady+api snehān* |na (tyajeyam ahaṃ* svayam Ctyajeyaṃ* mumukṣayā )|
children.translated_text: Even if, out of affection, I myself would not abandon my own people,
death will forcibly separate us from one another. ||6.44|
My mother, who bore me in her womb with great longing and suffering—

children.text: tasyā* niṣ+phala+yatnāyāḥ |kva*ahaṃ* mātuḥ kva sā mama ||6.45|
children.translated_text: her efforts now without fruit—where am I in relation to my mother, and where is she to me? ||6.45|
Just as birds come together on a roosting tree and then disperse,
so the meeting of beings is inevitably followed by separation. ||6.46|
Just as clouds come together and then again disperse,

children.text: saṃyogo* viprayogaś* ca |tathā me prāṇināṃ* mataḥ ||6.47|
children.translated_text: so too, in my view, is the union and separation of living beings. ||6.47|
Since this world passes on, deceiving one another,
attachment is not fitting when meetings are like a dream. ||6.48|
Trees are separated from their innate color of leaves;
will not the parting of one from another surely happen? ||6.49|

children.text: tad* evaṃ* sati saṃtāpaṃ* |mā kārṣīḥ saumya gamyatām |
children.translated_text: Therefore, this being so, do not grieve, O gentle one — go.

children.text: lambate yadi tu sneho* |gatvā*api punar* āvraja ||6.50|
children.translated_text: But if your affection lingers, then having gone, return again. ||6.50|
And tell the people in <s>Kapilavastu</s> not to be anxious on our account:
let attachment toward me be abandoned, and let them hear of my resolve. ||6.51|
Either he will swiftly return, having put an end to birth and death,
or, having failed in his purpose, without support, he will go to destruction." ||6.52|
Hearing his words, <s>Kanthaka</s>, the finest of horses,

children.text: jihvayā lilihe pādau |(bāṣpam Cvāṣpam )uṣṇaṃ* mumoca ca ||6.53|
children.translated_text: licked his feet with his tongue and shed warm tears. ||6.53|
With his hand, webbed, marked with the <s>svastika</s>,
and bearing a wheel in its center, the prince stroked him
and spoke to him as to a friend:
"Shed no tears, <s>Kanthaka</s>; this has shown your true horse-nature.
Be patient — this labor of yours will soon bear fruit." ||6.55|
Then that resolute one, grasping the jewel-hilted
sharp sword that was in <s>Chandaka</s>'s hand,
drew forth from its scabbard the blade adorned with golden work,
like a venomous serpent from its hole. ||6.56|
Drawing out that blade, dark blue as a blue lotus petal,
he cut off his beautiful hair together with its diadem,
and cast it, its wrappings scattering, into the sky
like a swan upon a lake. ||6.57|
Out of desire for worship and great respect,
the celestial beings seized it as it was flung;
and the hosts of gods in heaven duly
honored it with celestial distinctions. ||6.58|
Having abandoned the possession of ornaments like a wife,
and having made his head bereft of glory,
seeing his garment stamped with golden swans,
that resolute one desired a forest garment. ||6.59|
Then a celestial being in the guise of a hunter,
of pure nature, knowing his intention,
clad in saffron-colored robes, approached,
and the scion of the <s>Śākya</s> king addressed him: ||6.60|

children.text: na yujyate hiṃsram idaṃ* dhanuś* ca |
