children.translated_text: "Your saffron robe is auspicious, a banner of sages,

children.text: tat saumya yady* asti na saktir* atra |
children.translated_text: and this bow of yours, suited to violence, does not accord with it.
Therefore, O gentle one, if you have no attachment to it,
give this to me, and take this in return." ||6.61|
The hunter replied: "O granter of desires, with this indeed

children.text: arthas* tu śakra+upama yady* anena hanta |
children.translated_text: I gain the confidence of deer from afar and slay them.
But if you have need of this, O one like <s>Śakra</s> (Indra),
take it and give me this white one." ||6.62|
Then with the highest joy he received the forest garment

children.text: vyādhas* tu divyaṃ* vapur* eva bibhrat |
children.translated_text: and gave up the fine cloth;
but the hunter, assuming his divine form,
took the white garment and ascended to heaven. ||6.63|
Then both the prince and the horse-keeper
were amazed as he departed thus,
and even more so at the forest garment
they instantly conceived great reverence. ||6.64|
Then, dismissing <s>Chandaka</s>, whose face was tearful,
that bearer of fame, clad in saffron, resolute,
the great-souled one went toward the hermitage
like the king of stars veiled by twilight clouds. ||6.65|
Then, as his master, indifferent to kingship,
went to the forest of austerities in his faded garment,
the horse-keeper, throwing up his arms,
cried out bitterly and fell to the ground. ||6.66|
And looking back again, he wept aloud,
embracing the horse <s>Kanthaka</s> with his arms.
Then, hopeless, lamenting again and again,
he went toward the city with his body, not with his heart. ||6.67|
Now he brooded, now he wailed,
now he stumbled, now he fell;
thus journeying, grieving through devotion,
he performed many helpless gestures on the road. ||6.68|
Thus ends the sixth canto, named 'The Turning Back of <s>Chandaka</s>,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |6|
Seventh Canto. |7|
Then, having dismissed <s>Chandaka</s>, weeping and tearful,
detached, with his desire for the forest,
<s>Sarvārthasiddha</s> (He Whose Every Purpose Is Fulfilled), overpowering all with his beauty,
entered that hermitage as if it were a perfected realm. ||7.1|
That prince, walking like the king of beasts,
entered the deer-park like a deer.
Though bereft of royal splendor, by the splendor of his person
he captivated the eyes of all the hermitage dwellers. ||7.2|
Standing with yoke-poles in hand, just as they were,
the wheel-bearing householders with their wives, out of curiosity,
beheld him, like <s>Indra</s>, and did not go forward,
like draft-oxen with half-bowed heads. ||7.3|
<s>Brāhmaṇas</s> who had gone out for firewood,
returning with handfuls of kindling, flowers, and <s>kuśa</s> grass,

children.text: taṃ* draṣṭum īyur* na maṭhān abhīyuḥ ||7.4|
children.translated_text: though foremost in austerity and of resolved mind,
went to see him rather than returning to their huts. ||7.4|
Delighted peacocks uttered their cries,
as if raising their heads at seeing a dark rain-cloud;
and the deer, abandoning their grass, stood facing him
with restless eyes, as did those who lived among the deer. ||7.5|
Seeing that lamp of the <s>Ikṣvāku</s> lineage
blazing like the rising sun,
even though their milking was already done, the cows dedicated to oblations
let down their milk in newly aroused joy. ||7.6|
"This must be the eighth of the <s>Vasus</s>,
or perhaps one of the two <s>Aśvins</s> descended to earth" —
such loud exclamations arose there,
born from the wonder of the sages at the sight of him. ||7.7|
Like a second form of the bull among scribes (the Creator),

children.text: sa* dyotayām āsa vanaṃ* hi kṛtsnaṃ* |
children.translated_text: like the splendor of the world, both moving and still,
he indeed illuminated the entire forest,
as if the sun had descended by chance. ||7.8|
Then, duly honored and invited
by those hermitage-dwellers,
he returned their courtesies, that upholder of <s>Dharma</s>,
with a voice like a cloud bearing rain. ||7.9|
Desiring liberation himself, though the hermitage was filled
with people seeking heaven through meritorious deeds,
he, the resolute one, walked through that hermitage
observing its various austerities. ||7.10|
The gentle one, observing the transformations wrought by austerity
among the ascetics rich in austerity in that forest of austerity,
wishing to ascertain the truth, spoke thus
to a certain ascetic who was accompanying him: ||7.11|
"Since this is my first time seeing a hermitage,
and I do not know the rules of this way of <s>Dharma</s>,
therefore, you should be pleased to tell me
what resolve has led to your practice." ||7.12|
Then that twice-born one, a dweller in austerity,
to the bull of the <s>Śākyas</s>, of bull-like valor,
narrated to him in order
the various kinds of austerity and the fruit of austerity: ||7.13|
"Non-domestic food grown in water,
leaves, water, fruits, and roots alone —

children.text: bhinnās* tu te te tapasāṃ* vikalpāḥ ||7.14|
children.translated_text: this, according to tradition, is the livelihood of sages,
but the different modes of austerity are various. ||7.14|
Some live by gleaning, like birds;
some graze on grass like deer;
some live together with serpents,
having become ant-hills, as it were, in the forest wind. ||7.15|
Others have their sustenance obtained by the effort of grinding stones;
some eat food ground by their own teeth;
some cook for others first, and then
attend to their own needs if anything remains. ||7.16|
Some, with their matted locks wet with water,
pour oblations twice into the fire, preceded by <s>mantras</s>.
Some plunge into the waters like fish
and dwell there, their bodies scratched by turtles. ||7.17|
By austerities of such kinds, accumulated over time,
some go to heaven by one means, others to the world of men.
Through a painful path, happiness is approached,
for they say happiness is the root of <s>Dharma</s>." ||7.18|
Hearing words such as these
from that one rich in austerity, the calf of the bull among men,
though he had not yet seen the truth, was not content,
and gently said this to himself: ||7.19|
"Austerity is of many kinds and essentially painful,
and the fruit of austerity is chiefly heaven.
But all worlds are subject to change —
truly the effort of these hermitages is for something small. ||7.20|
Those who abandon dear ones, kin, and sensual objects,
and practice restraint for the sake of heaven —
they, separated and wishing to go further,
proceed only to yet another, greater bondage. ||7.21|
He who, through the bodily mortifications called 'austerity,'
seeks worldly activity for the sake of desire,
without examining the faults of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
he, through suffering, merely seeks more suffering. ||7.22|
Though beings are always terrified of death,
yet they strive for rebirth.
Though death is certain while this activity continues,
they are plunged into the very thing from which they are terrified. ||7.23|
Some enter upon hardship for the sake of this world,
others undergo toil for the sake of heaven;
for the sake of happiness, the world, miserable with desire and unfulfilled,

children.text: na khalv* ayaṃ* garhita* eva yatno* |
children.translated_text: falls into what is not its purpose at all. ||7.24|
This effort is not indeed to be despised
which, abandoning the lower, aims at the higher;

children.text: kāryaṃ* tu tad* yatra punar* na kāryam ||7.25|
children.translated_text: but with the same exertion, wise men should strive
for that goal where no further striving is needed. ||7.25|
If the mortification of the body is <s>Dharma</s>,
then the comfort of the body would be <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness).
But since one attains happiness in the next world through <s>Dharma</s>,
then <s>Dharma</s> here below would yield <s>adharma</s> as its fruit. ||7.26|
Since the body acts and ceases to act
under the control of the mind,
therefore the discipline of the mind alone is fitting,
for without the mind, the body is but a log of wood. ||7.27|
If merit is to be sought through purity of food,
then merit must belong to deer as well,
and also to those outcast men who,
through the fault of fortune, are turned away from fruits. ||7.28|
If the resolution to endure suffering is the cause of merit,
then surely the same resolution should apply to happiness too.
Or if resolution in regard to happiness has no validity,
then surely resolution in regard to suffering has no validity either. ||7.29|
Likewise those who, for the sake of purifying their <s>karma</s>,
touch waters, entering what they call a '<s>tīrtha</s>' (sacred ford) —
even there, the satisfaction is merely in the heart; for waters will not wash away sin." ||7.30|

children.text: spṛṣṭaṃ* hi yad* yad* guṇavadbhir* ambhas* |
children.translated_text: For whatever water has been touched by the virtuous

children.text: tat tat pṛthivyāṃ* yadi tīrtham iṣṭam |
children.translated_text: is deemed a holy <s>tīrtha</s> (pilgrimage ford) on earth;
therefore I regard virtues themselves as the true <s>tīrtha</s>,
for water is without doubt merely water. ||7.31|
Thus he spoke many things, well-reasoned,
and the sun went to its setting;
then, into that forest with trees discolored by sacrificial smoke,
tranquil in its austerities, he entered. ||7.32|
With the <s>agnihotra</s> (sacred fire) freshly kindled and blazing,
teeming with sages who had performed their ablutions,
with the deity-shrines humming with the murmur of <s>japa</s> (chanted prayers),
it seemed as if the ritual culmination of <s>dharma</s> was underway. ||7.33|
A few nights there, he who shone like the moon,
remained, examining their austerities;
and having surveyed and assessed all their austerities,
he departed from that ground of the ascetic field. ||7.34|
The hermitage-dwellers then followed him,
their minds captivated by his beauty and greatness,
as great sages would follow <s>dharma</s> departing
from a land overpowered by the ignoble. ||7.35|
Then he beheld those rich in austerity,
wearing matted locks, bark-garments, and ragged robes;
and, observing their austerities with respect,
he stood at the auspicious, glorious root of a tree. ||7.36|
Then the hermitage-dwellers approached
and stood surrounding that best of men;
and the eldest among them, with great deference,
spoke these words in a gentle and timely manner: ||7.37|
'When you arrived, the hermitage became as if full;
when you depart, it becomes as if empty.',
Therefore, dear one, you should not abandon this place,
as one who wishes to live should not abandon desired life. ||7.38|
The holy <s>Himālaya</s> mountain is nearby,
frequented by Brahma-sages, royal sages, and divine sages;
and the very austerities of the ascetics
are multiplied by its proximity. ||7.39|
And holy <s>tīrthas</s> on all sides likewise,
stepping-stones, as it were, to the firmament,
frequented by self-controlled, <s>dharma</s>-minded ones,
by divine sages and great sages. ||7.40|
Moreover, from here the northern direction especially
is suitable to frequent for the sake of spiritual distinction;
but it is not proper for a wise person
to proceed even a single step southward. ||7.41|
But if in this ascetic grove you have seen one who is inactive,
or one of mixed <s>dharma</s> who has fallen, or one who is impure,

children.text: dṛṣṭas* tvayā yena na te vivatsā |
children.translated_text: and on that account you do not wish to dwell here,
then tell us, so that the dwelling may be made pleasant. ||7.42|
For these ascetics desire as a companion in austerity
you, who are a veritable treasury of <s>tapas</s> (ascetic power);
for dwelling together with you, who are equal to <s>Indra</s>,
would bring the glory of <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.' ||7.43|
When thus addressed, in the midst of the ascetics,
by the chief of ascetics, that chief of the wise,
having made his vow for the destruction of <s>bhava</s> (worldly existence),
disclosed his inner intention: ||7.44|
'Among these sages, upright in soul, bearers of <s>dharma</s>,
who, from their beloved-guest nature, are like my own kinsmen,
through such sentiments directed toward me,
supreme delight has arisen in me, and a path has been shown. ||7.45|
By these affectionate, heart-penetrating
words, in brief, I feel as if bathed;
and my delight in the <s>dharma</s>, newly grasped,
is now stirred once again. ||7.46|
That I shall leave you, who are so worthy of refuge,
who have shown such exceeding partiality —
this causes me sorrow too,
just as when one abandons kinsmen. ||7.47|
But your <s>dharma</s> is directed toward heaven,
while my aspiration is for non-return to existence;

children.text: asmin vane yena na me vivatsā |
children.translated_text: therefore I do not wish to dwell in this grove,
for the <s>dharma</s> of cessation is different from that of continued activity. ||7.48|
Therefore it is neither displeasure nor any fault of yours
on account of which I wander away from this forest;
established in a <s>dharma</s> suited to a former age,
all of you are indeed like the great sages.' ||7.49|
Then, hearing the prince's words — truthful, meaningful,
very smooth yet powerful and majestic —
those ascetics
regarded him with special and great reverence. ||7.50|
A certain twice-born there, one who slept on ashes,
emaciated, with a topknot, wearing wooden-bark and rags,
yellowish-eyed, with a thin, long nose,
holding a water-pot in one hand, spoke these words: ||7.51|
'O wise one, noble indeed is your resolve,
that you, though young, have seen the fault in birth.
Having duly considered heaven and liberation,
he truly exists whose mind is set on liberation. ||7.52|

children.text: yajñais* tapobhir* niyamaiś* ca tais* taiḥ |
children.translated_text: Through various sacrifices, austerities, and restraints,
those who are passionate aspire to heaven;
but those who are strong, having fought passion as if it were an enemy,
seek <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). ||7.53|
If then this determination is fixed in you,
let your honor go quickly to the <s>Vindhya</s> region;
there dwells the sage <s>Arāḍa</s>,
who has gained vision of the ultimate good. ||7.54|
From him your honor will hear the path to truth,
and if it appeals, will follow it;
but as I perceive, this mind of yours
will go even beyond his doctrine, shaking it off. ||7.55|
For this face — with its clear, high nose, large, wide eyes,
copper-red lower lip, sharp white teeth,
and thin, red tongue —
will drink up the entire ocean of what is to be known. ||7.56|
The unfathomable depth that is yours,
the brilliance, and the auspicious marks —
you shall attain a mastership on earth
that was not attained even by the sages of former ages.' ||7.57|
'Excellent!' — and thus the prince,
having greeted that company of sages, departed;
and they, having duly attended upon him,
re-entered, those hermitage-dwellers, the ascetic grove. ||7.58|
Thus ends the seventh canto, entitled 'Entering the Ascetic Grove,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |7|
Canto Eight |8|
Then that horse-groom, heavy-hearted,
as his master departed thus into the forest, free from attachment,
strove to restrain his grief on the road,
yet even so his tears could not be checked. ||8.1|
The road that he had traveled in a single night
by his master's command, together with that steed,
that same road, brooding on his master's absence,
he traversed in eight days. ||8.2|
The horse <s>Kanthaka</s>, though powerful, walked sluggishly,
grew weary in spirit and lost his vigor;
though still adorned with his ornaments,
he seemed bereft of splendor, deprived of his master. ||8.3|
And turning back, facing the ascetic grove,
he neighed loudly and piteously, again and again;
though hungry on the road, he did not welcome nor take
grass or water, as he had before. ||8.4|
Then, to the city called <s>Kapilavastu</s>,
bereft of that great soul who sought the world's welfare,
those two arrived gradually, as if to an empty place,
like the sky deprived of the sun. ||8.5|
Though adorned with lotuses,
with waters beautified, and with trees bearing flowers,
that very pleasure-garden, resembling a forest,
did not shine, because the citizens had lost their joy. ||8.6|
Then, by men wandering about distractedly with downcast spirits,
their eyes dimmed and struck by tears,
those two, as if being held back, entered the city
slowly, as if bathed in dust. ||8.7|
And seeing those two, walking with drooping bodies,
returned without the bull of the <s>Śākya</s> clan,
the townspeople shed tears on the road,
as when the chariot of <s>Dāśarathi</s> (<s>Rāma</s>) returned of old. ||8.8|
Then the people, overcome with anger,
with tears, spoke to <s>Chandaka</s> on the road,
'Where is the prince, the joy of the city and the realm?
He has been abducted by you!' — and thus they followed behind. ||8.9|
Then he spoke to those devoted people:
'It is not I who abandoned the prince;

children.text: rudann* ahaṃ* tena tu nir+jane vane |
children.translated_text: rather, it was I who was weeping, and in that lonely forest
he dismissed me and my householder's garb.' ||8.10|

children.text: idaṃ* vacas* tasya niśamya te janāḥ |
children.translated_text: Hearing these words, those people
concluded, 'Truly this is exceedingly difficult!';
they could not hold back the water falling from their eyes,
and they reproached their own minds for having desired the reward. ||8.11|
Then they said, 'Let us enter today that very forest
to which he has gone, he of the gait of a lordly elephant;

children.text: jijīviṣā na*asti hi tena no* vinā |
children.translated_text: for there is no desire to live without him,
just as for embodied beings without their senses.' ||8.12|
'This city, forsaken by him, is a wilderness;

children.text: vanaṃ* ca tat tena samanvitaṃ* puram |
children.translated_text: and that forest, inhabited by him, is a city;

children.text: na śobhate tena hi no* vinā puraṃ* |
children.translated_text: for without him the city does not shine,
as heaven without <s>Indra</s> after the slaying of <s>Vṛtra</s>.' ||8.13|
Then, hearing 'The prince has returned!',
the women rushed to the latticed windows;
but seeing the horse's back was empty,
they shut the windows again and cried out. ||8.14|
The king, having undertaken a vow for the recovery of his son,
his mind oppressed by the vow and by grief,
chanted prayers in the temple,
and performed this and that ritual according to his wishes. ||8.15|
Then, with eyes filled with tears,
taking the horse and followed by the groom,
he entered the royal palace, stricken with grief,
as if his lord had been carried off by an enemy in battle. ||8.16|
And as he entered the palace of the king,
looking about with tear-streaming eyes,
<s>Kanthaka</s> neighed with a full-throated voice,
as if announcing the sorrow to the people. ||8.17|
Then the birds that roamed in the palace grounds
and the well-tended horses tethered nearby
echoed back the neigh of that horse,
suspecting it heralded the approach of the prince. ||8.18|
And the people, deceived by an excess of hope,
those near the inner quarters of the king,
hearing <s>Kanthaka</s> the horse neigh thus,
thought, 'Surely the prince is entering!' ||8.19|
Then, swooning between extreme joy and grief,
their eyes eager for a glimpse of the prince,
the women rushed forth from the house with hope,
like restless lightning from an autumn cloud. ||8.20|
With disheveled hair, soiled clothes and garments,
their faces without cosmetics, their eyes struck by tears,
the women, deprived of adornment, did not shine,
like stars in the sky, reddened at the end of night. ||8.21|
with feet reddened yet without anklets,
with faces without earrings, their necks straight,
with hips naturally full yet without girdles,
with breasts as if robbed, without necklaces or chest-bands — ||8.22|
beholding them with eyes brimming with tears,
and <s>Chandaka</s> and the horse without a master,
those excellent women, with despondent faces, wept aloud
like cows in the forest abandoned by the bull. ||8.23|
Then, with tears, <s>Gautamī</s>, the queen of the earth's lord,
tender as a buffalo-cow that has lost her calf,
stretching out her arms, fell to the ground
like a golden plantain with trembling leaves. ||8.24|
Others, their radiance dimmed, their arms slack at the shoulders,
the women, as if rendered lifeless by grief,

children.text: na cukruśur* na*aśru jahur* na śaśvasur* |
children.translated_text: neither cried out, nor shed tears, nor breathed;

children.text: na (celur* āsur* likhitā* Ccetanā* ullikhitā* )iva sthitāḥ ||8.25|
children.translated_text: they stood motionless, as if painted. ||8.25|
Other women, weakened, swooning with grief for their husband,
with faces streaming with torrents from their eyes,
bedewed their breasts, from which the sandalwood paste was washed away,
like mountain slopes wet with cascading springs. ||8.26|
And with their faces struck by the tear-water of their eyes,
that royal palace then gleamed
like a lake with lotuses, their flowing water beaten
by the cloud-rain in the season of fresh waters. ||8.27|
With well-rounded, plump, close-set fingers, unadorned,
their veins hidden — those excellent women
struck their breasts with lotus-like hands
like creepers shaken by the wind with their own tendrils. ||8.28|
And those women, with their uplifted breasts quivering from the blows of their hands,
appeared
like rivers with pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> (ruddy geese)
swaying on lotuses tossed by the forest breeze. ||8.29|
Just as their breasts pressed against their hands,
so too their hands were pressed against their breasts;
those weak and compassion-weary women inflicted mutual pain
upon their fingertips and breasts. ||8.30|
Then, her eyes reddened with rage,
her voice choked and hoarse with the accompaniment of grief,
<s>Yaśodharā</s>, her bosom heaving with sighs,
her deep sorrow streaming with tears, spoke: ||8.31|
"Having abandoned me, helpless, asleep in the night —
where has he gone, that chariot of my heart, O <s>Chandaka</s>?

children.text: upāgate ca tvayi kanthake ca me |
children.translated_text: And now that you have returned, and <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s> too,
while those three have departed together, my mind trembles! ||8.32|
Ignoble, heartless, and hostile was your deed toward me!
O cruel one, having done this, why do you weep now?
Restrain your tears; be satisfied in your mind —

children.text: na saṃvadaty* aśru ca tac* ca karma te ||8.33|
children.translated_text: your tears and your deed do not agree! ||8.33|
With one so dear, so obedient, so loyal, so good,
with you as companion, fulfilling his purpose,
the noble prince has gone, never to return —
rejoice! For your labor has borne fruit! ||8.34|
Better for a man to have a discerning enemy
than an ignorant, treacherously skillful friend;
for by you, calling yourself a friend but lacking wisdom,
this great calamity has been brought upon this family. ||8.35|
For pitiable are these women, their ornaments cast aside,
their red eyes clouded with flowing tears,
who, though their husband still lives as firm as the <s>Himavat</s>,
are bereft of beauty, like widows. ||8.36|
And these palace-rows, their balcony-arms flung out,
resounding with the long cooing of doves,
separated from him together with the women's quarters,
weep aloud, as it were. ||8.37|
Desiring harm for all these people surely
is this horse <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s> too;

children.text: jahāra sarva+svam itas* tathā hi me |
children.translated_text: for he carried away my all from here,
like a thief of jewels in the night while people slept. ||8.38|
Since he is indeed capable of enduring the blows of arrows,
how much more the blows of a whip —
how then did this one, from fear of the whip's fall,

children.text: śriyaṃ* gṛhītvā hṛdayaṃ* ca me samam ||8.39|
children.translated_text: depart, carrying away my glory and my heart alike? ||8.39|
He who does this ignoble deed now neighs loudly,
as if filling the royal palace with his sound;

children.text: yadā tu nirvāhayati sma me priyaṃ* |
children.translated_text: but when he was carrying away my beloved,
then that vilest of horses was mute! ||8.40|
For if he had neighed, awakening the people,
or had made a sound on the ground with his hooves,
or had uttered a great champing of his jaws —
then such suffering as this would not have been mine!" ||8.41|
Hearing this piteous lamentation of the queen,
her words knotted with tears, halting,
<s>Chandaka</s>, head bowed, tearful, with joined palms,
slowly uttered this reply: ||8.42|
"Do not blame <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s>, O Queen,

children.text: na ca*api roṣaṃ* mayi kartum arhasi |
children.translated_text: nor should you direct your anger at me.
Know us both to be wholly without fault;

children.text: gato* nṛ+devaḥ sa* hi devi devavat ||8.43|
children.translated_text: for the divine prince has departed as a god, O Queen. ||8.43|
For I, though knowing the king's command,

children.text: balāt kṛtaḥ kair* api daivatair* iva |
children.translated_text: was compelled as if by some divine power,
and swiftly brought this horse,
and followed untiring on the road. ||8.44|
This excellent horse too, as he went, did not touch
the ground with his hoof-tips, as if held in mid-air;
and likewise, as if by divine decree, his mouth restrained,
he neither made a champing sound nor neighed. ||8.45|
When the prince went out,
the gate opened of its own accord,
and the darkness of night was split as if by the sun —
therefore let this be understood as divine ordinance. ||8.46|
When, despite the king's command, the watchful people
in the house and city, by the thousands,
were at that time carried off by sleep and did not awaken —
therefore let this be understood as divine ordinance. ||8.47|
And when a garment suited for forest-dwelling
was given to him at that time by a celestial being,
and his crown, cast into the sky, was received there —
therefore let this be understood as divine ordinance. ||8.48|
Therefore, O divine queen, you should not find fault
with his departure in the two of us;
there was no free will, neither in me nor in this horse —
for he departed escorted by the gods." ||8.49|
Hearing of that wondrous departure, attended by many divine signs,
those women of that great-souled one
lost their grief, as it were, and were filled with wonder;
but from his going forth, they suffered a fever of the heart. ||8.50|
Then <s>Gautamī</s>, her eyes unsteady and swimming with grief,
distressed like a <s>kurarī</s> (osprey) that has lost her young,
abandoning her composure, wailed aloud
and spoke, her face bathed in tears: ||8.51|
"Those locks of his, with great waves, soft, dark, and beautiful,
each growing from its own root, rising high,
those tresses of his cast upon the ground,
worthy of being encircled by a king's diadem! ||8.52|
With long arms, with the gait of the king of beasts,
with great bull-like eyes, with a golden blazing radiance,
with a broad chest, with a voice deep as a thundering kettledrum —
does one of such a nature deserve to dwell in a hermitage? ||8.53|
This earth is surely without good fortune,
having lost that supreme lord of noble deeds;
for one so virtuous — such a king
is born through the merit of his subjects. ||8.54|
Those feet, with well-formed, webbed toes, soft,
with hidden ankles, tender as lotus-stalk blossoms —
how will those two feet, with wheel-marks in the center,
tread upon the hard forest ground? ||8.55|
That body, accustomed to reclining on couches atop palaces,
honored with costly garments, <s>aguru</s> (aloe), and sandalwood —
how will that powerful body fare in the forest
in the coming of cold and heat and rain? ||8.56|
He who was proud with lineage, character, strength, splendor,
learning, fortune, and youth,
accustomed only to giving, never to begging —
how will he go about begging for alms from others? ||8.57|
Having slept on a pure, golden bed,
awakened at night by the sounds of musical instruments —
how, alas, will my vow-observing one now sleep
upon the bare ground, covered by a mere piece of cloth?" ||8.58|
Hearing this piteous lament,
those women, embracing each other with their arms,
shed water from their eyes
like creepers shaken loose, dropping honey from their blossoms. ||8.59|
Then <s>Yaśodharā</s> fell upon the ground
like a <s>cakravākī</s> (ruddy goose) separated from her mate;

children.text: śanaiś* ca tat tad* vilalāpa viklavā |
children.translated_text: slowly, she lamented this and that, distraught,
again and again, with a voice choked and halting: ||8.60|
"If he wishes to practice the <s>Dharma</s> by abandoning me,
his <s>sahadharmacarinī</s> (partner in religious life), helpless —
what kind of <s>Dharma</s> is his, when he wishes to enjoy
austerity without his partner in <s>Dharma</s>? ||8.61|
Surely he does not hear of those former kings,
his ancestors, beginning with <s>Mahāsudarśa</s>,
who went to the forests accompanied by their wives —
for thus he wishes to practice <s>Dharma</s> without me! ||8.62|
Or does he not see in the sacrifices, properly performed by Vedic rites,
both husband and wife consecrated together?
Both equally desiring to share the fruit in the hereafter —
therefore jealousy of <s>Dharma</s> has arisen in him against me! ||8.63|
Surely, knowing that I am devoted to the <s>Dharma</s>,
and that my mind is often in conflict through jealousy of my beloved,
fearlessly leaving me, the angry one, at ease —
he wishes to seize the <s>Apsarases</s> in the world of great <s>Indra</s>! ||8.64|

children.text: iyaṃ* tu cintā mama kī+dṛśaṃ* nu tā* |
children.translated_text: But this is my thought: what kind of beauty
and virtues of form do the women there possess,
that he practices austerities in the forest for their sake,

children.text: śriyaṃ* ca hitvā mama bhaktim eva ca ||8.65|
children.translated_text: abandoning both his glory and my devotion? ||8.65|

children.text: na khalv* iyaṃ* svarga+sukhāya me spṛhā |
children.translated_text: Truly, I have no longing for the happiness of heaven;
that is not hard to attain even for a person of self-control.

children.text: sa* tu priyo* mām iha vā paratra vā |
children.translated_text: But that my beloved should not abandon me, here or hereafter —

children.text: kathaṃ* na jahyād* iti me mano+rathaḥ ||8.66|
children.translated_text: that is my heart's desire. ||8.66|
If I am too unfortunate to gaze upon the face
of my husband, with his long eyes and pure smile,
then surely this ill-fated <s>Rāhula</s> too does not deserve
even once to turn in his father's lap. ||8.67|
Ah, how cruel and exceedingly harsh
is the heart of that resolute one of tender beauty,
who abandons such an infant son
whose babbling speech would delight even an enemy! ||8.68|
Indeed, my heart too must be exceedingly hard,
made of stone or even of iron,
that it does not break, left helpless, bereft of glory, accustomed to happiness —

children.text: vanaṃ* gate bhartari yan* na dīryate ||8.69|
children.translated_text: does not break when her husband has gone to the forest. ||8.69|
Thus the queen, faint with grief for her husband,
wept, brooded, and lamented again and again;
though by nature steadfast, that virtuous woman, through sorrow,

children.text: dhṛtiṃ* na sasmāra cakāra na*u hriyam ||8.70|
children.translated_text: remembered neither fortitude nor even modesty. ||8.70|
Then, seeing <s>Yaśodharā</s>, distraught with grief and lamentation,
fallen upon the ground,
the women cried out with tear-stained faces,
like great lotuses beaten by rain. ||8.71|
The king, meanwhile, having completed his recitations and performed the auspicious fire offerings,
came forth from the temple of the gods;
struck by the anguished cry of the people,
he staggered like an elephant struck by a thunderbolt. ||8.72|
And learning of <s>Chandaka</s> and <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s> both,
and hearing of his son's firm resolve,
the lord of the earth, stricken with grief, fell down
like the banner of <s>Śakra</s> (Indra) when the festival is over. ||8.73|
Then, for a moment bewildered by grief for his son,
supported by people of equal birth,
gazing at the horse with eyes filled with tears,
the king, standing on the ground, lamented: ||8.74|
"Having done many dear things for me in battle,
a great unkindness has been done by you, O <s>Kaṇṭhaka</s>;

children.text: guṇa+priyo* yena vane sa* me priyaḥ |
children.translated_text: for my dear one, who loved virtue, was carried by you to the forest—
though dear, you have acted as an enemy. ||8.75|

children.text: tad* adya māṃ* vā naya tatra yatra sa* |
children.translated_text: Therefore, either take me today to where he is,

children.text: vraja drutaṃ* vā punar* enam ānaya |
children.translated_text: or go swiftly and bring him back again;

children.text: ṛte hi tasmān* mama na*asti jīvitaṃ* |
children.translated_text: for without him there is no life for me,
as without the right medicine for one afflicted with a deep disease. ||8.76|
When <s>Suvarṇaṇiṣṭhīvin</s> was taken by death,
that <s>Saṃjaya</s> did not die was difficult indeed;
but I, when my son devoted to <s>Dharma</s> has gone,
wish to release my self, as if without self-mastery. ||8.77|
Of the mighty <s>Prajāpati</s> who established the ten royal families,
the knower of past and future, born of <s>Vivasvat</s>—
when even <s>Manu</s> was deprived of his virtuous, beloved son,

children.text: kathaṃ* na muhyed* *dhi mano* manor* api ||8.78|
children.translated_text: how should not even <s>Manu's</s> mind be confounded? ||8.78|
I envy <s>Aja</s>, that wise king, lord of men,
companion of <s>Indra</s>;

children.text: gate vanaṃ* yas* tanaye divaṃ* gato* |
children.translated_text: when his son went to the forest, he went to heaven,
and did not live on wretchedly with futile tears. ||8.79|
Tell me, good friend, of that hermitage court

children.text: hṛtas* tvayā yatra sa* me jala+añjaliḥ |
children.translated_text: to which you have taken my water-oblation (my son);
for these my vital breaths, thirsting, desire to seek him,
wishing to go the way of the dead." ||8.80|
Thus the king, his grief born of separation from his son,
having cast aside the innate fortitude befitting the earth,
like <s>Daśaratha</s>, overcome by grief for <s>Rāma</s>,
lamented profusely, nearly senseless. ||8.81|
Then the counselor of wisdom and the aged family priest,
both endowed with the qualities of learning, discipline, and virtue,
spoke to him these measured words, as was fitting—

children.text: na ca paritapta+mukhau na ca*apy* a+śokau ||8.82|
children.translated_text: their faces neither scorched with heat nor without sorrow: ||8.82|
"Abandon your grief, O best of men, and come to fortitude;
O steadfast one, you should not shed tears like one of weak resolve.
Many kings on earth have abandoned their glory
like a trampled garland, and gone to the forests. ||8.83|

children.text: api ca niyata* eṣa* tasya bhāvaḥ |
children.translated_text: Moreover, this destiny of his is fixed—
remember the words of the sage <s>Asita</s> of old;

children.text: na hi sa* divi na cakra+varti+rājye |
children.translated_text: for he cannot be made to dwell happily even for a moment
in heaven or in a universal sovereign's kingdom. ||8.84|

children.text: yadi tu nṛ+vara kārya* eva yatnas* |
children.translated_text: But if, O best of men, effort must indeed be made,
speak quickly—so that we may go there;
let there be a contest of many kinds here

children.text: tava tanayasya vidheś* ca tasya tasya ||8.85|
children.translated_text: between your son and that destiny of his. ||8.85|
Then the king commanded them:
'Go quickly, the two of you, from this very place;

children.text: na hi mama hṛdayaṃ* prayāti śāntiṃ* |
children.translated_text: for my heart will not find peace,
like a forest bird longing for its young.' ||8.86|
'So be it,' and at the command of the lord of men,
the counselor and the priest went to that forest;
and the king, together with the women and his wife,
attended to the remaining duties. ||8.87|
Thus ends the eighth canto, named 'The Lamentation of the Inner Apartments,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |8|
Ninth Canto |9|
Then those two—the counselor and the priest,
urged on by the king with the goad of tears,
like two noble horses goaded with every effort,
went swiftly to that forest with the speed of affection. ||9.1|
Arriving at that hermitage, weary from their journey, those two,
with a suitable retinue, at the proper time,
having set aside royal pomp and with humble bearing,
went directly to the dwelling of <s>Bhārgava</s>. ||9.2|
Having duly honored that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>,
and being honored by him in fitting manner,
they took their seats, and addressing <s>Bhārgava</s> seated on his seat,
breaking off other talk, they spoke of their own business: ||9.3|
"Of a king of pure energy, of pure and far-reaching fame,
born of the <s>Ikṣvāku</s> lineage—
may the venerable one know this person as learned
in the reception of scripture and in the grasp of sacred counsel. ||9.4|
His son, like <s>Jayanta</s> to that <s>Indra</s>-like king,
desiring to cross beyond the fear of old age and death,
has come here, it is said, for that purpose;
may the venerable one know that we two have come on his account." ||9.5|
He said to them: "That long-armed prince
has indeed come, and has not failed to understand;
knowing that 'this <s>Dharma</s> involves return' (is cyclical),
he has gone, desiring liberation, toward <s>Arāḍa</s>." ||9.6|
Then, having ascertained the truth from him,
those two, bidding farewell to that <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> at that very moment,
though weary, as if unwearied through devotion to the king,
hastened in the direction he had gone. ||9.7|
Going on, they then beheld him, devoid of adornment,
blazing with his own radiance,
seated at the foot of a tree by the path,
like the sun entered into the expanse of a cloud. ||9.8|
Then, leaving his vehicle, the priest approached him
together with the bearer of sacred counsel,
as the sage <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>, son of <s>Ūrvaśī</s>,
together with <s>Vāmadeva</s>, approached <s>Rāma</s> dwelling in the forest. ||9.9|
They honored that worthy one,
as <s>Śukra</s> and <s>Aṅgiras</s> honor great <s>Indra</s> in heaven;
and he in turn honored those worthy ones,
as great <s>Indra</s> in heaven honors <s>Śukra</s> and <s>Aṅgiras</s>. ||9.10|
Having received permission, those two then sat
beside the banner of the <s>Śākya</s> family;
and they shone in his proximity
like the twin stars <s>Punarvasu</s> near the moon in conjunction. ||9.11|
Seated at the tree-root, blazing,
the priest addressed the prince
as <s>Bṛhaspati</s> addresses <s>Jayanta</s>, son of <s>Śakra</s>,
seated in heaven beneath the <s>Pārijāta</s> tree: ||9.12|
"With the arrow of grief for you deeply lodged in his heart,
having fallen to the ground in a swoon for a moment,
O prince, the king, with a rain of tears from his eyes—

children.text: yat tvām avocat tad* idaṃ* nibodha ||9.13|
children.translated_text: hear what he said to you: ||9.13|
'I know your firm resolve regarding <s>Dharma</s>,
and I understand that this goal of yours is destined;
but I am burning, as if by a fire equal to fire,
from your untimely resort to the forest. ||9.14|
Therefore come, O lover of <s>Dharma</s>, for my sake who love you;
for the sake of <s>Dharma</s> itself, abandon this intention;
for this torrent of grief, swollen,
strikes me like a river's current against its bank. ||9.15|
The action of wind, sun, fire, and thunderbolt
upon clouds, water, forests, and mountains—
that very action grief performs upon us,
by tearing, drying up, burning, and splitting. ||9.16|
Therefore, enjoy sovereignty over the earth for now;
you shall go to the forest at the time seen in the scriptures.
Show regard for me, your unwilling kinsman—
for compassion toward all beings is indeed <s>Dharma</s>. ||9.17|

children.text: na ca*eṣa* dharmo* vanae* eva siddhaḥ |
children.translated_text: And this <s>Dharma</s> is not attained only in the forest;
perfection is certain even in the city for the self-controlled.

children.text: buddhiś* ca yatnaś* ca nimittam atra |
children.translated_text: Wisdom and effort are the means here;

children.text: vanaṃ* ca liṅgaṃ* ca hi bhīru+cihnam ||9.18|
children.translated_text: the forest and the ascetic's garb are but the marks of the timid. ||9.18|
By lords of men wearing diadems, with garlands hanging from their shoulders,
with arms clasped by armlets,
reclining in the lap of <s>Lakṣmī</s> (prosperity)—
even by such householders has the <s>Dharma</s> of liberation been attained. ||9.19|
The two younger brothers of <s>Dhruva</s>—<s>Bali</s> and <s>Vajrabāhu</s>,
<s>Vaibhrāja</s>, <s>Āṣāḍha</s>, and <s>Antideva</s>,
and likewise <s>Janaka</s>, the king of <s>Videha</s>,
and the son of King <s>Senajit</s>— ||9.20|
know these kings as householders
who were accomplished in the discipline of <s>Dharma</s> leading to the highest good;
therefore, embrace both at once—
mastery of wealth and royal splendor.' ||9.21|
'I desire to embrace you tightly,
just after your consecration, still wet with the waters,
gazing up at the royal parasol held over you,
and with that very joy, to enter the forest.' ||9.22|
"Thus spoke the lord of the earth to you,
in words with syllables knotted by tears;
having heard, you should, for the sake of pleasing him,
follow his love with your own love. ||9.23|
In the fathomless flood of grief born from you,
the <s>Śākya</s> king is drowning in an ocean of suffering;
therefore, rescue him who is without a protector,
like a ship rescuing one drowning without refuge in the sea." ||9.24|
"Hearing that by <s>Bhīṣma</s>, born from the womb of <s>Gaṅgā</s>,
by <s>Rāma</s> (Paraśurāma), and by <s>Rāma</s> (Dāśarathi) of the <s>Bhārgava</s> lineage,
deeds were performed for the sake of pleasing the father,

children.text: pitus* tvam apy* arhasi kartum iṣṭam ||9.25|
children.translated_text: you too should do what is desired by your father. ||9.25|
Go to the queen who raised you,
who has not departed to the quarter favored by <s>Agastya</s> (the south, i.e., death);
like an affectionate cow whose calf is lost,
she is constantly distressed, weeping pitifully. ||9.26|
Like a female swan separated from the male swan,
like a she-elephant abandoned by the bull in the forest,
your bride, afflicted, though having a protector yet protectorless—
you should save her by your sight. ||9.27|
Your one son, a child, suffering undeserved pain,
bearing grief inwardly,
free that <s>Rāhula</s> from the sorrow of separation from kin,
as the full moon from the eclipse of <s>Rāhu</s>. ||9.28|
By the fire of grief, fueled by your absence,
with sighs as its smoke, darkness as its flame—
burning, it seeks the water of your sight—
both the inner chambers and the entire city. ||9.29|
That <s>Bodhisattva</s>, of perfect being,
having heard the words of that priest,
reflected for a moment—he who knew qualities, on what was said with quality—
and replied with these humble words: ||9.30|
"I understand the feelings of fathers toward a son,
especially those of the king toward me;
yet knowing well the perils of disease, old age, and calamity,
but out of fear, with no other course, I abandon my own people.

children.text: draṣṭuṃ* priyaṃ* kaḥ sva+janaṃ* hi na*icchen* |
children.translated_text: For who would not wish to see his beloved family,
if there were no separation from the beloved at the end?
But since separation comes even after long togetherness,
therefore I abandon even my venerable and affectionate elder.
And the grief that you say the king feels on my account—

children.text: śokaṃ* bhavān (āha na tat Carhati na )priyaṃ* me |
children.translated_text: that is not pleasing to me,
that he torments himself over meetings that are like dreams,
when separation is inevitable.

children.text: evaṃ* ca te niścayam etu buddhir* |
children.translated_text: Therefore, let your mind come to this firm conclusion,
having seen the varied course of the world:
neither a son nor a kinsman is the cause of anguish;
this suffering is caused by ignorance alone.
Just as for travelers meeting together on a road,
separation is certain at the appointed time for beings—

children.text: prājño* janaḥ ko* nu bhajeta śokaṃ* |
children.translated_text: what wise person would embrace grief,

children.text: bandhu+(pratijñāta+janair* vihīnaḥ Cpriyaḥ sann* api bandhu+hīnaḥ )||9.35|
children.translated_text: though bereft of those acknowledged as kinsmen?
One departs from here, leaving one's own people in the next world;
and having been deceived here, one departs again;
and having gone there too, one goes elsewhere—
thus, for a being that is always departing, what attachment?
Since from the womb onward,
in all states, death pursues to kill—
why has your honor, who loves his son, spoken to me
of my forest-resort being untimely?
There may be an untimely moment for the pursuit of sense-pleasures,
and a proper time is prescribed for the acquisition of wealth;
but time drags along the world through all times—
for the supreme good that leads to fulfillment, there is no fixed time.

children.text: rājyaṃ* mumukṣur* mayi yac* ca rājā |
children.translated_text: And as for the kingdom that the king wishes to bestow upon me—

children.text: tad* apy* udāraṃ* sa+dṛśaṃ* pituś* ca |
children.translated_text: that too is noble and befitting a father;
but it is not fitting for me to accept,
like unwholesome food for a sick person, out of greed.
How could kingship, the abode of delusion,
be suitable for a wise man to undertake,
where there is anxiety, intoxication, and toil,
and the affliction of <s>Dharma</s> through wrongdoing against others?
A golden palace that is on fire,
the finest food mixed with poison,
a lotus pond infested with crocodiles—
for indeed, kingship is charming yet the resort of misfortune.

children.text: ((Citthaṃ* ca rājyaṃ* na sukhaṃ* na dharmaḥ C))|
children.translated_text: Thus kingship is neither happiness nor <s>Dharma</s>;
just as in the past, kings who developed revulsion,
when unavoidable suffering came with advancing age,
abandoning their kingdoms, went to the very forest.
Better indeed to eat grass in the forest,
embracing supreme contentment like a jewel,
than to dwell together with the easily obtained
faults of royal splendor, like unseen black serpents.
Praiseworthy indeed it is for kings, abandoning kingdoms,
to enter the forest with desire for <s>Dharma</s>;
but it is not fitting for one who has broken his vow
to abandon the forest and enter a household.

children.text: ((Cjātaḥ kule ko* hi naraḥ sa+sattvo* C))|
children.translated_text: What man of noble birth and character,
having entered the forest with desire for <s>Dharma</s>,
would cast aside the ascetic's robe, abandoning shame,
and take refuge in the city of even <s>Purandara</s> (<s>Indra</s>)?
For he who, out of greed, delusion, or fear,
would again take up vomited food—
he, out of greed, delusion, or fear,
having abandoned desires, would take them up again.
And he who, having somehow escaped from a burning house,
would enter it again—
he, having abandoned household life with its faults seen,
would through delusion desire to take it up again.
And the scripture that says householder kings
attained liberation—that is not so;
for where is the <s>Dharma</s> of liberation, whose essence is tranquility,
and where is the <s>Dharma</s> of kings, whose essence is punishment?
If one delights in tranquility, then the kingdom is lax;
if the mind is on the kingdom, then tranquility is destroyed;

children.text: ((Cśamaś* ca taikṣṇyaṃ* ca hi na*upapannaṃ* C))|
children.translated_text: for tranquility and severity are incompatible,
like the unity of cold and hot, water and fire.
Therefore, either those lords of the earth
surely attained tranquility by abandoning their kingdoms,
or, though connected with kingship, through restraint of their senses,
they had a false sense of non-final liberation.
Let tranquility be properly theirs while in kingship—
I have not come to the forest without firm resolve;
for having cut the bond called household-kinship,
freed, I do not wish to enter it again."
Having heard the son of the king speak
in a manner befitting his quality of self-knowledge,
free from longing, reasoned, and powerful—
the minister too spoke in reply:
"This resolve of yours regarding the way of <s>Dharma</s>—

children.text: na*ayaṃ* na yukto* na tu kāla+yuktaḥ |
children.translated_text: it is not unfitting, but it is not suited to the time.
Having given your aged father to grief,

children.text: syād* dharma+kāmasya hi te na dharmaḥ ||9.53|
children.translated_text: this would be not <s>Dharma</s> for you who desire <s>Dharma</s>.
Surely your intelligence is not very subtle,
or undiscerning regarding <s>Dharma</s>, wealth, and pleasure;
for you who go, having dismissed a present good,
for the sake of an unseen result.
Some say there is rebirth;
others, of firm assertion, say there is none;
since this matter is thus in doubt,
therefore it is fitting to enjoy the prosperity that is at hand.
If there is indeed any future existence,
we shall enjoy ourselves there according to our birth;
but if there is no further existence at all,
then liberation of this world is accomplished without effort.
Some speak of the next world as existing,
but they do not describe a method for liberation;
just as heat is the nature of fire, and fluidity of water—
so too they call natural tendency the nature in the process of existence.
Some explain from inherent nature (<s>svabhāva</s>)
both the good and the bad, and both existence and non-existence;
since all this is natural,
therefore effort too is futile.
That the activity of the senses is fixed,
and that there is pleasantness and unpleasantness in sense-objects,
and that one is connected with old age and sufferings—

children.text: kas* tatra yatno* nanu sa* sva+bhāvaḥ ||9.59|
children.translated_text: what effort is there in that? Is it not inherent nature?
The sacrificial fire is extinguished by water,
and fires bring water to evaporation;
the elements, being distinct, residing in bodies,
having come to unity, support the world.
That the form of hands, feet, belly, back, and head
develops in the womb—

children.text: yad* ātmanas* tasya ca tena yogaḥ |
children.translated_text: and that the self has a connection with that—
those who know call that natural.
Who makes the sharpness of a thorn,
or the varied nature of beasts and birds?
All this has proceeded from inherent nature;
there is no free will—whence then effort?
Others speak of creation as from a Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>);
then what purpose has the effort of man?
Whatever cause brings about the arising of the world,
that same cause is certainly the cause of its cessation.
Some say that the self alone is the cause
of both arising and the destruction of existence;
but they say arising happens without effort,
while they declare liberation to be attained through effort.
A man becomes free from debt to ancestors through offspring,
to sages through the <s>Vedas</s>, to the gods through sacrifices;
he is born together with these three debts—
whoever has liberation, his liberation is indeed thus.
Thus, by this prescribed sequence of duties,
those who know speak of liberation as requiring effort;
and even those who strive through this sequence,
the seekers of liberation, attain only weariness.

children.text: tat saumya mokṣe yadi bhaktir* asti |
children.translated_text: Therefore, O gentle one, if you are devoted to liberation,
follow the prescribed method properly as stated;
thus there will be the attainment of this,
and the destruction of anguish for the king.
And the thought that has arisen in you about the faults
of entering a dwelling from the ascetic groves—

children.text: tatra*api cintā tava tāta mā bhūt |
children.translated_text: let there be no anxiety about that, my son,
for even in the past, some went from the forests to their own homes.
King <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, though dwelling in the ascetic grove,
chosen by his subjects, went to the city;
likewise <s>Rāma</s>, coming from the ascetic grove,
protected the earth that was being wronged by ignoble ones.
Likewise, the overlord of <s>Śālva</s>, called <s>Druma</s>,
entered the city from the forest together with his son;
and <s>Āntideva</s>, son of <s>Sāṃkṛti</s>, though become a <s>Brahmarṣi</s> (Brahmin sage),
from the sage <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>, accepted royal splendor.
Those of such kind, blazing with <s>Dharma</s> and fame,
having abandoned forests, entered their homes;
therefore there is no fault in going home
from the ascetic grove for the sake of <s>Dharma</s>."
Then, hearing those words of the minister,
which were dear and beneficial, and like eyes to the king,
complete, orderly, unattached, and unhurried—
the king's son, firm in resolve, spoke these words:
"This doubt of 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' here—
my certainty in this matter is not from the words of others;
having ascertained the truth through austerity and tranquility,
I myself shall grasp whatever is certain here.
It is not fitting for me to grasp a view born of doubt,
struck by the conflicting opinions of those unclear;
for what wise person would go on the trust of another,
like a blind man among the blind, led by a blind guide?
But though I have not yet seen the truth,
when the good and bad are in doubt, my mind inclines to the good;
for even futile effort is better for one of good soul
than pleasure for one of contemptible soul.
But seeing this scriptural tradition as unsettled,

children.text: yad* uktam āptais* tad* avehi sādhv* iti |
children.translated_text: know as good what has been spoken by the trustworthy;
and know that trustworthiness means the state of having abandoned faults,
for one who has abandoned faults will not speak what is untrue.

children.text: gṛha+praveśaṃ* prati yac* ca me bhavān |
children.translated_text: And regarding what you said to me about returning home,
citing the examples of <s>Rāma</s> and others—

children.text: na te pramāṇaṃ* na hi dharma+niścayeṣv* |
children.translated_text: they are not authoritative, for in matters of determining <s>Dharma</s>,
those whose vows have been impaired are not sufficient as authority.

children.text: tad* evam apy* eva ravir* mahīṃ* pated* |
children.translated_text: Therefore, even if the sun were to fall to the earth,
even if the <s>Himavān</s> mountain were to abandon its firmness—
one who has not seen the truth, with senses directed toward objects,

children.text: śrayeya na tv* eva gṛhān pṛthag+janaḥ ||9.78|
children.translated_text: an ordinary person — I would never return to the household life. ||9.78|
I would enter a blazing fire
rather than enter a home without having accomplished my goal.'
Thus he made his vow, resolute,
and rising, free from attachment, he departed as he wished. ||9.79|
Then those two, the minister and the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, both in tears,
hearing his firm resolve,
with dejected faces, following him in sorrow,
slowly, having no other course, returned to the city. ||9.80|

children.text: tat+snehād* atha nṛ+pateś* ca bhaktitas* tau |
children.translated_text: Out of affection for him and out of devotion to the king,
they went back with backward glances and kept stopping;
like the sun, resplendent with its own radiance, hard to withstand,

children.text: taṃ* draṣṭuṃ* na hi pathi śekatur* na moktum ||9.81|
children.translated_text: they could neither bear to look at him on the road, nor to let him go. ||9.81|

children.text: tau jñātuṃ* parama+gater* gatiṃ* tu tasya |
children.translated_text: In order to learn the course of him who sought the supreme goal,
they stationed trustworthy secret agents,
and saying, 'How shall we face the king
who yearns for his beloved son?' — they departed somehow. ||9.82|
Thus ends the ninth canto, entitled 'The Search for the Prince,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |9|
Canto Ten |10|
That royal scion, broad and full of chest,
having left behind those two charged with oblations and <s>mantras</s>,
crossing the <s>Gaṅgā</s> with its rolling waves,
went to the splendid city of <s>Rājagṛha</s>. ||10.1|
Well-guarded and adorned by mountains,

children.text: dhṛtaṃ* ca pūtaṃ* ca śivais* tapo+daiḥ |
children.translated_text: upheld and purified by auspicious ascetics,
he entered the city marked by five hills,
serene, like the Self-Existent One entering the summit of heaven. ||10.2|
Perceiving his depth, his vigor,
and his radiant form surpassing all men,
the people there were amazed at that time,
as at the bull-bannered <s>Śiva</s> when observing the vow of standing still. ||10.3|

children.text: taṃ* prekṣya yo* *anyena yayau sa* tasthau |
children.translated_text: He who was going elsewhere, seeing him, stood still;
he who was standing there on the road, followed him;

children.text: drutaṃ* yayau (yaḥ sa* jagāma dhīraṃ* Csa+dayaṃ* sa+dhīraṃ* )|
children.translated_text: he who was going fast, went slowly and gently;

children.text: yaḥ kaś+cid* āste sma sa* ca*utpapāta ||10.4|
children.translated_text: whoever was sitting, sprang up. ||10.4|
Some people honored him with joined palms,
some reverently saluted him with bowed heads,
some greeted him with affectionate words —
no one went past without paying homage. ||10.5|
Seeing him, those in colorful attire felt ashamed;
those of scattered speech fell silent on the road;
as if <s>dharma</s> itself were visibly near,
no one harbored an unjust thought. ||10.6|
Whether women or men on the royal road,
even those engaged in other activities, with great reverence,
gazing at that god-like son of a king,
their sight was never sated. ||10.7|
Whether his eyebrows, his forehead, his face, his eyes,

children.text: vapuḥ karau vā caraṇau gatiṃ* vā |
children.translated_text: his body, his hands, his feet, or his gait —

children.text: yad* eva yas* tasya dadarśa tatra |
children.translated_text: whatever part anyone beheld there,
that very part bound that person's gaze. ||10.8|
And seeing him with the <s>ūrṇā</s>-mark between his brows, large-eyed,
with a blazing body, with auspicious web-markings on his hands,
worthy of ruling the earth, yet in the garb of a mendicant —
the glory of <s>Rājagṛha</s> was agitated. ||10.9|
Then <s>Śreṇya</s>, the lord of the <s>Magadha</s> domain,
from an outer palace-terrace, saw the vast throng of people
and asked the reason for it;
thereupon a man reported to him: ||10.10|
'He who, the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> said, would attain either
supreme knowledge or sovereignty of the earth —
he, the son of the lord of the <s>Śākyas</s>,
is being gazed upon by the people, having gone forth as a mendicant.' ||10.11|
Then the king, having heard the matter, his mind fixed upon it,
spoke to that very man:
'Let it be known where he goes';
and with 'So be it,' the man followed him. ||10.12|
With steady gaze, looking only a yoke's-length ahead,
with restrained speech, walking slowly and deliberately,
that best of mendicants went about collecting alms,
having stilled his limbs and his restless mind. ||10.13|
And having received alms as they came,
he went to a secluded mountain spring;
having duly eaten there,
he ascended Mount <s>Pāṇḍava</s>. ||10.14|
On that fresh, <s>lodhra</s>-grove-enfolded mountain,
in a bower filled with the cries of peacocks,
he, the hero among men, in saffron robes, shone
like the young sun upon the summit of the eastern mountain. ||10.15|
There, that royal servant, having spotted him,
reported to King <s>Śreṇya</s>;
and that king, having heard, out of great respect,
proceeded there with a small retinue. ||10.16|
He, equal in valor to the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s>, ascended <s>Pāṇḍava</s>,
that supreme mountain, he of mountain-like stature,
a crown-bearer, of lion-like gait, a lion among men,
like a lion with flowing mane, ascended. ||10.17|
Then, on its very peak,
he saw the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, with senses stilled,
seated in the cross-legged posture, radiant,
like the moon rising from a mass of clouds. ||10.18|
Seeing him seated there, by beauty of form and serenity,
as if the very embodiment of <s>dharma</s>,
that king of men, with wonder and humility,
approached him, as <s>Śakra</s> (Indra) approaches the Self-Existent One. ||10.19|
Having duly met that foremost knower of propriety,
he inquired about his health and the balance of his constitution;
and he too replied with fitting courtesy,
assuring the king of his well-being and freedom from illness. ||10.20|
Then, on a clean, blue-black rock-slab,
like an elephant's ear, the king sat down;
and having sat, with his permission,
wishing to know his purpose, he spoke thus: ||10.21|
'My affection for your family is great,
inherited and also tested;
a desire to speak has arisen in me on account of my own years —
therefore hear these words of affection. ||10.22|
Your family, beginning with <s>Āditya</s> (the Sun), is vast,

children.text: navaṃ* vayo* dīptam idaṃ* vapuś* ca |
children.translated_text: your age is young, and this form is radiant;
why is this mind of yours, out of the natural order,
delighted in begging rather than in kingship? ||10.23|
This body of yours deserves red sandalwood,
not the touch of saffron robes;
this hand is fit for the protection of subjects,
not worthy of eating food given by others. ||10.24|

children.text: tat saumya rājyaṃ* yadi paitṛkaṃ* tvaṃ* |
children.translated_text: Therefore, gentle one, if you do not wish
your father's kingdom, out of affection for your father, through force,
and if your mind cannot endure the succession,
then quickly enjoy half of my domain. ||10.25|
Thus there would be no oppression of your own people,
and glory, resting on tranquility, would come in due course;
therefore, accept my friendship,
for the prosperity of the good should be shared with the good. ||10.26|
But if, through pride of lineage,
there is no quality of trust in you toward us,
then plunge into drawn-up battle formations with arrows,
and with me as your ally, conquer enemies! ||10.27|
Therefore, choose one or another course;
pursue <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s> (wealth), and <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) in proper order;
for those who neglect the <s>trivarga</s> (three aims of life), confusing them through passion,
suffer downfall both in the next world and in this. ||10.28|
For the <s>kāma</s> that oppresses <s>artha</s> and <s>dharma</s>,
or the <s>artha</s> that scorns <s>dharma</s> and <s>kāma</s>,
or the <s>dharma</s> that is pursued through the abandonment of <s>kāma</s> and <s>artha</s> —
all of those should be rejected, if one desires the true goal. ||10.29|
Therefore, through the cultivation of the three aims,
make this form of yours fruitful;
for the complete attainment of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, and <s>kāma</s>
is called the complete goal of human life. ||10.30|
You should not render fruitless these two
full arms, worthy of drawing a bow;
for like <s>Māndhātṛ</s>, they are fit to conquer

children.text: (lokān api trīn iha Clokāni hi trīṇi hi )kiṃ* punar* gām ||10.31|
children.translated_text: even the three worlds here, let alone the earth! ||10.31|
I say this truly out of affection,
not from a desire for sovereignty, nor from conceit;

children.text: imaṃ* hi dṛṣṭvā tava bhikṣu+(veṣaṃ* Cveśaṃ* )|
children.translated_text: for seeing this mendicant garb of yours,
compassion has arisen in me, and even tears have come. ||10.32|
While this beauty, befitting your lineage,
has not yet been conquered by old age —
enjoy pleasures now, O you who desire the mendicant's stage;

children.text: Pādas ab and cd are exchanged in C.

children.translated_text: in due time you shall practice the beloved <s>dharma</s>.
An aged man can indeed attain <s>dharma</s>,
but old age has no access to the enjoyment of pleasures;
therefore they prescribe pleasures for the young,
wealth for the middle-aged, and <s>dharma</s> for the old. ||10.34|
For in this world of the living, the periods of youth
are enemies of both <s>dharma</s> and <s>artha</s>;
even when guarded, they are hard to control,
for the pleasures carry them away by that path. ||10.35|
Aged periods of life are capable of deliberation,
steady, inclined to remaining and dwelling;
with little effort they become tranquil of nature,
even unavoidably, through modesty. ||10.36|
Therefore, having passed beyond youth — which is fickle,
pleasure-dominated, heedless, impatient, short-sighted,
and full of deceptions —
people breathe easy, as if having crossed a wilderness. ||10.37|
Therefore, let this youth first pass away —
unsteady, fickle, heedless as it is;
for youth is the prime target of <s>Kāma</s> (desire)
and cannot be guarded from the senses. ||10.38|
But if your wish is indeed for <s>dharma</s> alone,
then perform sacrifice — that is the <s>dharma</s> of your lineage;
for through sacrifices, having attained the summit of heaven,
even <s>Indra</s> himself went to that summit.' ||10.39|
With arms bitten by golden armlets,
with crowns brilliant with jewel-lamps and colorfully adorned,

children.text: nṛ+pa+ṛṣayas* tāṃ* hi gatiṃ* gatā* makhaiḥ |
children.translated_text: royal sages have gone to that destination through sacrifices
which the great sages reached through austerity. ||10.40|
Thus spoke the lord of <s>Magadha</s>,

children.text: yaḥ samyag* vala+bhid* iva (bruvan babhāse Cdhruvaṃ* babhāṣe )|
children.translated_text: who spoke truly as if <s>Indra</s> himself, the cleaver of <s>Vala</s>;
but hearing it, that prince did not waver,
like Mount <s>Kailāsa</s> with its many colorful peaks. ||10.41|
Thus ends the tenth canto, entitled 'The Visit of <s>Śreṇya</s>,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>, composed by <s>Aśvaghoṣa</s>. |10|
Canto Eleven |11|
Then, thus addressed by the lord of <s>Magadha</s>
with words friendly in manner but contrary in substance,
self-possessed, unchanged, pure in the purity of his lineage,
the son of <s>Śuddhodana</s> spoke these words: ||11.1|
It is no wonder for your honor to speak thus,
born as you are in the great lineage of the lion-marked ones;
and if this should be your conduct, O friend-seeker,
toward one who is your friend, of purified conduct — ||11.2|
friendship with the unworthy, following one's own family,
does not endure, like fortune among the feeble;
the tradition of affection established by forefathers
is what the good augment. ||11.3|
Those people in the world who share in the enterprises
of their friends in times of material hardship —
those I consider true friends;

children.text: sva+sthasya vṛddhiṣv* iha ko* hi na syāt ||11.4|
children.translated_text: for who would not be a friend when a person is prosperous and well? ||11.4|

children.text: evaṃ* ca ye dravyam avāpya loke |
children.translated_text: And those in the world who, having obtained wealth,
employ it for friends and for <s>Dharma</s> —
such wealth, having gained its essence,
does not cause anguish when lost in the end. ||11.5|
And, O King, out of friendship and nobility

children.text: (khalv* eṣa* yo* māṃ* prati niścayas* Cvibhāvya mām eva viniścayas* )te |
children.translated_text: this determination of yours toward me is clear;
I shall address you in the spirit of friendship itself —
I would not say any other answer here. ||11.6|
Having understood the fear of old age and death,
I have embraced this <s>Dharma</s> out of the desire for liberation,
leaving behind dear kinsmen with tear-stained faces —
how much more so pleasures, which are the causes of misfortune! ||11.7|
I do not fear venomous serpents so much,
nor thunderbolts fallen from the sky,
nor fires accompanied by wind,
as I fear sensual pleasures. ||11.8|
For pleasures are impermanent, thieves of what is wholesome,
empty, and resembling illusions in this world;
even when merely hoped for, they delude
the minds of men — how much more when they are present! ||11.9|
Those overcome by desires do not attain happiness
even in the third heaven, alas, let alone in the mortal world;
for one who thirsts, there is no satiation from desires,
just as fire with wind as its friend is not sated by fuel. ||11.10|
In the world, there is no misfortune equal to desires,

children.text: mohāc* ca teṣv* eva janaḥ prasaktaḥ |
children.translated_text: yet from delusion people are attached to them;
knowing this truth, one who fears misfortune —
what wise man would of his own accord crave misfortune? ||11.11|
Even having gained the ocean-girdled earth,
they desire to cross to the far shore of the great ocean;
the world has no satisfaction from desires,
like the ocean has none from falling waters. ||11.12|
Even when a god rained down a shower of gold,
even having conquered all four continents,
and even having obtained half the seat of <s>Śakra</s> (Indra) —
<s>Māndhātṛ</s> was not sated in his pleasures. ||11.13|
Even having enjoyed the kingdom of the gods in heaven,
when <s>Śatakratu</s> (Indra) had fled from fear of <s>Vṛtra</s>,
and even having yoked great sages in his arrogance —
<s>Nahuṣa</s>, unsated in his desires, fell. ||11.14|
And <s>Aiḍa</s> (Purūravas), the king, having entered the triple heaven,
and even having won the goddess <s>Urvaśī</s>,
out of greed wished to steal gold from the sages
and went to ruin, unsated in pleasures. ||11.15|
From <s>Bali</s>, the great <s>Indra</s>; from <s>Nahuṣa</s>, the great <s>Indra</s>;
and <s>Indra</s> again from <s>Nahuṣa</s> — those who rose and fell —
in heaven or on earth, in those pleasures
tossed by the waves of fortune — who would place his trust? ||11.16|
Wearing bark-cloth garments, subsisting on roots, fruits, and water,
bearing matted locks long as serpents —
even sages, occupied with other matters, were broken by them;
who then would seek those foes called desires? ||11.17|
And <s>Ugra</s>, mighty-weaponed, fierce in wielding his weapon,
for whose sake he met death more terrible than <s>Bhīṣma</s>'s —
even the thought of them is inauspicious and deadly
for the well-conducted, let alone for those without vows. ||11.18|
Considering the small taste in sensual pleasures,
the excess of bondage, the insatiability,

children.text: sadbhyaś* ca garhāṃ* niyataṃ* ca pāpaṃ* |
children.translated_text: the censure from the good, and the certainty of sin —
who would take that poison called desire? ||11.19|
Hearing of the suffering of those devoted to desires,
afflicted by plowing and other labors,
and seeing the well-being of those free from curiosity about pleasures —
it is fitting for the self-possessed to abandon desires. ||11.20|
The fulfillment of desires should be known as calamity, O lover of desires;
for when desires are fulfilled, one attains intoxication,
and from intoxication one does what should not be done, not what should,
and thereby, wounded, one goes to a bad destiny. ||11.21|
Those desires which, obtained and guarded with great effort,
deceive and depart again and again —
among these, which provoke anger even when solicited,
what wise man would take delight in desires here? ||11.22|
Having sought and seized them, inflamed with thirst,
those who cannot abandon them experience suffering;
in those desires that resemble torches of grass in this world,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.23|
Those without self-mastery, bitten by them in the heart,
seek destruction and do not attain happiness;
in those desires that resemble angry, fierce serpents,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.24|
Like dogs tormented by hunger gnawing at bones,
even after partaking of them, one is never satisfied;
in those desires that resemble dry skeletal bones,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.25|
Those that cause suffering because they are shared in common
with kings, thieves, water, and fire —
in those desires that resemble cast-away pieces of meat,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.26|
Where for those who possess them, ruin comes from all sides,
from enemies and even from kinsmen —
in those harmful desires that are like dwellings,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.27|

children.text: girau vane ca*apsu ca sāgare ca |
children.translated_text: On mountains, in forests, in waters, and in the ocean,
those who leap for them fall to ruin;
in those desires that resemble fruits at the top of a tree,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.28|
Obtained through intense and various exertions,
they perish here in a moment;
in those desires that resemble enjoyments in a dream,

children.text: Verses 11.29 and 11.30 are exchanged in ed. C.

children.translated_text: what self-possessed person would take delight?
Those which, even when honored, nurtured, and guarded,
bring no happiness —
in those desires that resemble a pit of burning coals,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.30|
The <s>Kurus</s> went to destruction on their account,
and the <s>Vṛṣṇi-Andhakas</s>, the <s>Maithilas</s>, and the <s>Daṇḍakas</s>;
in those desires that resemble slaughter-house stakes and swords,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.31|
On their account, the <s>Asuras</s> <s>Sunda</s> and <s>Upasunda</s>,
driven by mutual enmity, perished;
in those desires that sever bonds of friendship,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.32|

children.text: (yeṣāṃ* kṛte vāriṇi pāvake Ckāma+andha+saṃjñāḥ kṛpayā va ke

children.translated_text: abandon themselves in water, fire,
For their sake, blinded by desire, some out of wretchedness,
or among flesh-eating beasts;
in those inauspicious desires that are like rivals,
what self-possessed person would take delight? ||11.33|
A fool acts pitiably for the sake of desire,
and meets with suffering, killing, imprisonment, and the like;
wretched with longing, the suffering one, for the sake of desire,
endures death and toil in the world of the living. ||11.34|
Deer are lured by songs to their slaughter,
moths fall into fire for the sake of form,
fish swallow the iron hook for the sake of bait —
therefore, sensual objects bear misfortune as their fruit. ||11.35|

children.text: kāmās* tu bhogā* iti (yan* matiḥ Cyan* mataṃ* )syād* |
children.translated_text: If it be thought that desires are enjoyments —
no enjoyments whatsoever are to be counted;
for material properties such as clothing in this world
should be understood as remedies against suffering. ||11.36|
Water is desired for quenching thirst,
food likewise for the removal of hunger,
a house for protection from wind, heat, and rain,
clothing for covering modesty and warding off the cold. ||11.37|
Likewise a bed for the removal of fatigue from sleep,
a vehicle for the removal of weariness from travel,
likewise a seat for the relief of standing,
bathing for cleanliness, health, and strength. ||11.38|
Since the objects of the senses exist as means of counteracting suffering,
they are not truly enjoyments for people;
who that is wise would declare, 'I enjoy pleasures,'
when engaged in the procedure of remedying suffering? ||11.39|
One who, being consumed by the burning of bile,
would designate the cooling treatment as an 'enjoyment' —
he, engaged in the procedure of remedying suffering,
would apply the word 'enjoyment' to desires. ||11.40|
And since there is no absoluteness in desires,
for this reason too I do not call them enjoyments;

children.text: yae* eva bhāvā* hi sukhaṃ* diśanti |
children.translated_text: for the very things that bestow happiness
are the same ones that bring suffering again. ||11.41|
Heavy garments and light garments alike
bring comfort in cold but discomfort in heat;
moonbeams and sandalwood paste, pleasant in heat,
bring comfort but become painful in cold. ||11.42|
Since pairs of opposites cling to everything in the world,
beginning with loss and gain —
therefore there is no person of unmixed happiness,
nor of unmixed suffering on this earth. ||11.43|
Seeing this mixture of happiness and suffering,

children.text: rājyaṃ* ca dāsyaṃ* ca mataṃ* samānam |
children.translated_text: kingship and servitude seem the same to me;

children.text: nityaṃ* hasaty* eva hi na*eva rājā |
children.translated_text: for a king does not always laugh,
nor does a slave always grieve. ||11.44|
Since the exercise of command is paramount in kingship,
therefore the sufferings of kings are great;
for a king is like a stake in a gate,
wearing himself out for the sake of the world. ||11.45|
If a king places trust in a kingdom where friends are treacherous
and many, he is ruined;
but if he trusts no one at all,
what happiness is there for a king who is fearful? ||11.46|
And when, even having conquered the entire earth,
one sees only a single city as fit for dwelling,
and even there, only a single palace to inhabit —
is not the state of being a king merely toil for the sake of others? ||11.47|
Even a king has but one pair of garments,
and just a measure of food for the stilling of hunger,
and likewise one bed and one seat —
the other distinctions of a king serve only his intoxication. ||11.48|
And if contentment is the desired fruit,
even without a kingdom I have contentment;
and when contentment exists for a man in this world,
surely all distinctions become indistinguishable. ||11.49|
Therefore I am not to be led astray toward desires,
having entered the secure, auspicious path;

children.text: smṛtvā su+hṛttvaṃ* tu punaḥ punar* māṃ* |
children.translated_text: but remembering your friendship again and again,
I say: 'Keep your promise!' ||11.50|

children.text: na* hy* asmy* amarṣeṇa vanaṃ* praviṣṭo* |
children.translated_text: For I have not entered the forest out of resentment,
nor with my crown struck off by an enemy's arrows,
nor with desire for those who have superior fruits;
therefore I do not accept your words. ||11.51|
One who, having released an angry, biting serpent,
would resolve to seize it again,
or, having dropped a blazing torch of grass —
he alone might return to desires once abandoned." ||11.52|
Would one who can see long for the blind,
or one who is free long for the bound, or a wealthy man for the destitute,
or one of sound mind for one of deranged mind?
Would such a one long for the life of sensual objects? ||11.53|
One who lives on alms is not to be pitied;
he is accomplished, wishing to cross beyond the fear of old age and death.
Here he has the supreme happiness of peace,
and hereafter his sufferings are ended. ||11.54|
But one who, though living in great prosperity,
is overcome by craving — he is to be pitied;
for he attains neither the happiness of peace here,
and hereafter he is seized by suffering. ||11.55|
It is fitting indeed for you to speak thus,
in keeping with your courage, conduct, and lineage;
and it is fitting for me to uphold a pledge
in keeping with my courage, conduct, and lineage. ||11.56|
For I, pierced by the arrow of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence),
have gone forth, wishing to attain peace.
I would not desire kingship even in the triple heaven —
how much less, alas, among mortals, where nothing is free from affliction! ||11.57|
As for your saying to me, O king, that the pursuit of the three goals (<s>trivarga</s>) in full

children.text: paro* manuṣya+artha* iti tvam āttha mām |
children.translated_text: is the supreme purpose of human life —

children.text: an+artha* ity* (eva mama*atra darśanaṃ* Cāttha mama*artha+darśanaṃ* )|
children.translated_text: my view of this is that it is purposeless,

children.text: kṣayī tri+vargo* hi na ca*api tarpakaḥ ||11.58|
children.translated_text: for the three goals are perishable and never satisfying. ||11.58|

children.text: pade tu yasmin na jarā na (bhīr* na ruṅ* Cbhīrutā )|
children.translated_text: But the state where there is no old age, no fear, no disease,
no birth, no cessation, and no anxiety —
that alone I consider the supreme purpose of a person,

children.text: na vidyate yatra punaḥ punaḥ kriyā ||11.59|
children.translated_text: where there is no repeated action again and again. ||11.59|
As for your saying, 'Wait for old age;
youth passes into change' —
this is uncertain, for it is seen that things are fickle:
old age too is unsteady, and youth can be firm. ||11.60|
When the Destroyer, skilled in his own work,
