children.text: vayaḥsu (sarveṣv* a+vaśaṃ* vikarṣati Csarveṣu ca saṃvikarṣati )|
children.translated_text: drags away the world helplessly at every age,
how, when the time of destruction is uncertain,
should a wise person seeking peace wait for old age? ||11.61|
When Death stands like a merciless hunter,
with old age as his weapon and disease as his scattered arrows,
striking the creatures that are like deer in the forest of destiny —
what hope is there for a long span of life? ||11.62|
Therefore, whether one is young, old, or a child,
one ought to act here with urgency,
so that for one who is righteous and self-disciplined,
the desired course — whether engagement or renunciation — may be attained. ||11.63|
And as for your saying, 'Perform the sacrifice,
the rite befitting your lineage, which has illustrious fruit, for the sake of <s>Dharma</s>' —

children.text: namo* makhebhyo* na hi kāmaye sukhaṃ* |
children.translated_text: I pay homage to sacrifices, but I do not desire the happiness
that is sought through causing suffering to another. ||11.64|
For to kill another creature, helpless, out of desire for the fruit —
this is not fitting for one who is compassionate in nature.

children.text: kratoḥ phalaṃ* yady* api śāśvataṃ* bhavet |
children.translated_text: Even if the fruit of sacrifice were everlasting,

children.text: tathā*api kṛtvā kim (u yat kṣaya+ātmakam Cupakṣaya+ātmakam )||11.65|
children.translated_text: even then, how much less when it is perishable by nature! ||11.65|

children.text: bhavec* ca dharmo* yadi na*a+paro* vidhir* |
children.translated_text: And if there were no other method of attaining <s>Dharma</s>
through vows, conduct, or mental tranquility,
even then one ought not to resort to sacrifice
in which the fruit is said to come from slaughter. ||11.66|
Even while a person dwells here in this world,
the pleasure that arises through harming others
is undesirable to one who is compassionate and wise —
how much more, alas, that which is unseen in the next life! ||11.67|
And I am not to be deceived into engaging in worldly activity for the sake of fruit;

children.text: bhaveṣu rājan ramate na me manaḥ |
children.translated_text: my mind takes no delight in worldly existences, O king.
Like creepers struck by the rain from a cloud,
all worldly activities are everywhere unstable. ||11.68|
I have come here with the desire to see
the sage <s>Arāḍa</s>, who teaches liberation.
I depart this very day; O king, may auspiciousness be yours.
Forgive my words, which are harsh through their devotion to truth. ||11.69|
May you protect like <s>Indra</s>, may you shine forever like the sun,

children.text: guṇair* ava śreya* iha*ava gām ava |
children.translated_text: may you protect with virtues, may you protect welfare here, may you protect the earth,
may you protect life through noble deeds, may you protect good sons,

children.text: śriyaś* ca rājann* ava dharmam ātmanaḥ ||11.70|
children.translated_text: and may you protect glory, O king, and may you protect the <s>Dharma</s> of yourself. ||11.70|
Just as the twice-born (a bird), born between the creation and destruction by the enemy of cold (fire),
goes forth, releasing its body,
so, between the slayers of the enemy of cold (between birth and death),
go forth, liberating your mind. ||11.71|
The king, with palms joined, his longing aroused, said:
"May you obtain what you desire without obstacle.
Having attained this fulfillment of purpose in due time,
you must show favor to me as well." ||11.72|
Having firmly promised 'So be it' to the king,
he then went to the hermitage of <s>Vaiśvantara</s>.
Amazed, watching him depart on his wandering,

children.text: nṛ+po* *api (vavrāja puriṃ* giri+vrajam Cca prāpur* imaṃ* giriṃ* vrajan )||11.73|
children.translated_text: the king too returned to his city, <s>Girivraja</s> (Rājagṛha). ||11.73|
Thus ends the eleventh canto, named 'The Censure of Desire,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s> composed by <s>Aśvaghoṣa</s>. |11|
Twelfth Canto. |12|
Then the moon of the <s>Ikṣvāku</s> race, seeking the hermitage
of the sage <s>Arāḍa</s>, who dwelt in tranquility, entered, as if filling it with his beauty. ||12.1|
Greeted from afar with a loud 'Welcome!'
by that one of the same <s>gotra</s> (lineage) as <s>Kālāma</s>, he approached. ||12.2|
Having duly asked each other about the equilibrium of bodily elements
and other matters, those two — noble, pure, and vigorous — sat down in a clean spot. ||12.3|
To the prince seated there, that best of sages
spoke, drinking him in, as it were, with two gazes wide with reverence: ||12.4|

children.text: viditaṃ* me yathā saumya |niṣkrānto* bhavanād* asi |
children.translated_text: "It is known to me, O gentle one, how you

children.text: chittvā snehamayaṃ* pāśaṃ* |pāśaṃ* dṛpta* iva dvi+paḥ ||12.5|
children.translated_text: departed from your palace, having cut the bond of affection like a proud elephant snapping its chain. ||12.5|

children.text: sarvathā dhṛtimac* ca*eva |prājñaṃ* ca*eva manas* tava |
children.translated_text: Your mind is entirely resolute

children.text: yas* tvaṃ* prāptaḥ śriyaṃ* tyaktvā |latāṃ* viṣa+phalām iva ||12.6|
children.translated_text: and wise, for you have arrived, having abandoned royal glory as if it were a vine bearing poisoned fruit. ||12.6|
It is not surprising that kings of advanced age
have gone to the forest, having given their wealth to their children, like a garland already worn and cast aside. ||12.7|

children.text: idaṃ* me matam āścaryaṃ* |nave vayasi yad* bhavān |
children.translated_text: But this, in my view, is wonderful — that you,
in the freshness of youth, without even having enjoyed royal glory, have arrived here, though standing amid the realm of sensual objects. ||12.8|

children.text: tad* vijñātum imaṃ* dharmaṃ* |paramaṃ* bhājanaṃ* bhavān |
children.translated_text: Therefore, you are the supreme vessel for knowing this <s>Dharma</s>;
having mounted the raft of knowledge, swiftly cross the ocean of suffering. ||12.9|

children.text: śiṣye yady* api vijñāte |śāstraṃ* kālena (varṇyate Cvartate )|
children.translated_text: Although the doctrine is taught to a known disciple in due time,

children.text: gāmbhīryād* vyavasāyāc* ca |(na parīkṣyo* Csu+parīkṣyo* )bhavān mama ||12.10|
children.translated_text: because of the depth and resolve, you are not in need of testing by me. ||12.10|
Understanding these words of <s>Arāḍa</s>,
that bull among men was supremely delighted and spoke this reply: ||12.11|
"This supreme graciousness of yours,
even toward one who is detached — though I have not yet attained my purpose, I feel as if fulfilled by it. ||12.12|

children.text: didṛkṣur* iva hi jyotir* |yiyāsur* iva daiśikam |
children.translated_text: For I regard my meeting with you

children.text: tvad+(darśanam Cdarśanād* )ahaṃ* manye |titīrṣur* iva ca plavam ||12.13|
children.translated_text: as a person desiring light regards a lamp, one wishing to travel regards a guide, and one wishing to cross regards a raft. ||12.13|

children.text: tasmād* arhasi tad* vaktuṃ* |vaktavyaṃ* yadi manyase |
children.translated_text: Therefore, if you think it should be told,
you should be pleased to tell me how a person
is liberated from old age, death, and disease." ||12.14|
Then <s>Arāḍa</s>, impelled by the prince's greatness alone,
set forth in brief the conclusion of his own doctrine: ||12.15|

children.text: yathā bhavati saṃsāro* |yathā (ca*eva nivartate Cvai parivartate )||12.16|
children.translated_text: "Hear this, our established conclusion, O best of listeners —

children.text: prakṛtiś* ca vikāraś* ca |janma mṛtyur* jarā*eva ca |
children.translated_text: how <s>saṃsāra</s> comes into being, and how it ceases: ||12.16|

children.text: tat tāvat sattvam ity* uktaṃ* |sthira+sattva parehi (tat Cnaḥ )||12.17|
children.translated_text: <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) and its modifications (<s>vikāra</s>),
birth, death, and old age — all this is called <s>sattva</s> (being); understand this, O one of firm being. ||12.17|

children.text: pañca bhūtāny* ahaṃ+kāraṃ* |buddhim a+vyaktam eva ca ||12.18|
children.translated_text: Know that what is called <s>prakṛti</s>, O knower of nature,

children.text: vikāra* iti (budhyasva Cbuddhiṃ* tu )|viṣayān indriyāṇi ca |
children.translated_text: consists of the five elements, <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego), <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), and the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest). ||12.18|

children.text: pāṇi+pādaṃ* ca vādaṃ* ca |pāyu+upasthaṃ* tathā manaḥ ||12.19|
children.translated_text: And understand as modifications (<s>vikāra</s>): the sense objects, the sense organs, hands, feet, speech, the anus, the reproductive organ, and the mind (<s>manas</s>). ||12.19|

children.text: asya kṣetrasya vijñānāt |kṣetra+jña* iti saṃjñi ca |
children.translated_text: From the knowledge of this field, one is called the 'knower of the field' (<s>kṣetrajña</s>);
and those who reflect upon the self (<s>ātman</s>) speak of the self as the <s>kṣetrajña</s>. ||12.20|
<s>Kapila</s>, together with his disciples, is known here as 'the awakened one' (<s>pratibuddha</s>);

children.text:
sa+(putro* *a+pratibuddhas* tu Cputraḥ pratibuddhaś* ca )|prajā+patir* iha*ucyate
               ||12.21|
children.translated_text: while his son, the unawakened, is called <s>Prajāpati</s> here. ||12.21|

children.text: jāyate jīryate ca*eva |(bādhyate Cbudhyate )mriyate ca yat |
children.translated_text: That which is born, grows old,

children.text: tad* vyaktam iti vijñeyam |a+vyaktaṃ* tu viparyayāt ||12.22|
children.translated_text: is afflicted, and dies — that is to be known as the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>); the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>) is the opposite. ||12.22|
Ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), and craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>)

children.text:
sthito* *asmiṃs* tritaye (jantus* Cyas* tu )|tat sattvaṃ* (na*ativartate
               Cna*abhivartate )||12.23|
children.translated_text: are to be known as the causes of <s>saṃsāra</s>; a being established in these three does not transcend that state of being. ||12.23|
Through wrong conviction (<s>vipratyaya</s>), through ego (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>), through confusion (<s>saṃdeha</s>), through identification (<s>abhisaṃplava</s>),
through non-discrimination (<s>aviśeṣa</s>), through lack of means (<s>anupāya</s>), through attachment (<s>saṅga</s>), and through falling (<s>abhyavapāta</s>) — ||12.24|
Among these, what is called wrong conviction (<s>vipratyaya</s>)
operates in a perverted manner: one does the wrong thing, one thinks what should be thought about differently. ||12.25|

children.text: bravīmy* aham ahaṃ* vedmi |gacchāmy* aham ahaṃ* sthitaḥ |
children.translated_text: 'I speak, I know, I go, I stand' —
such ego (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) thus operates where there is no self. ||12.26|

children.text: yas* tu (bhāvān a+saṃdigdhān Cbhāvena saṃdigdhān )|ekī+bhāvena paśyati |
children.translated_text: But one who sees things that are undoubted as one single entity,
like a lump of clay, without doubt — that, here, is called confusion (<s>saṃdeha</s>). ||12.27|

children.text: ya* eva*ahaṃ* sa* eva*idaṃ* |mano* buddhiś* ca karma ca |
children.translated_text: 'I myself am this — mind, intellect, and action;

children.text:
yaś* (ca*eva*eṣa* Cca*evaṃ* sa* )gaṇaḥ so* *aham |iti yaḥ so* *abhisaṃplavaḥ
               ||12.28|
children.translated_text: and this aggregate, that is I' — one who thinks thus, that is identification (<s>abhisaṃplava</s>). ||12.28|
One who, O knower of distinctions, does not distinguish between the awakened and the unawakened,

children.text: prakṛtīnāṃ* ca yo* veda |so* *a+viśeṣa* iti smṛtaḥ ||12.29|
children.translated_text: and among the various natures — he is known as non-discriminating (<s>aviśeṣa</s>). ||12.29|
Salutations, sacrificial exclamations, sprinkling, consecration, and the like —
these are proclaimed by the wise as lack of means (<s>anupāya</s>), O knower of means. ||12.30|
That by which the foolish person becomes attached through the actions of mind, speech, and intellect
to sensual objects, without detachment — that is known as attachment (<s>abhiṣvaṅga</s>). ||12.31|
'This is mine; I belong to this' — the suffering that one imagines thus
is to be known as falling (<s>abhyavapāta</s>), by which one falls into <s>saṃsāra</s>. ||12.32|

children.text:
ity* a+(vidyāṃ* Cvidyā )hi (vidvān sa* Cvidvāṃsaḥ [??] )|pañca+(parvāṃ* Cparvā
               )samīhate |
children.translated_text: Thus the wise know this ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) to have five branches;
darkness (<s>tamas</s>), delusion (<s>moha</s>), great delusion (<s>mahāmoha</s>), and the twofold gloom (<s>tāmisra</s>). ||12.33|

children.text: tatra*ālasyaṃ* tamo* viddhi |mohaṃ* mṛtyuṃ* ca janma ca |
children.translated_text: Know sloth therein as darkness, and delusion as death and birth;

children.text: mahā+mohas* tv* a+saṃmoha |kāma ity* (eva gamyatām Cavagamyatām )||12.34|
children.translated_text: but great delusion is to be understood as freedom from delusion, and as desire.

children.text: yasmād* atra ca bhūtāni |pramuhyanti mahānty* api |
children.translated_text: Since great beings too become deluded herein,
therefore, O mighty-armed one, this is known as 'great delusion.'
And 'darkness' (<s>tāmisra</s>), O one free from anger, they call anger itself;
and 'blinding darkness' (<s>andhatāmisra</s>), O one free from despair, they call despair.
A fool, conjoined with this fivefold ignorance,
is anointed into births in <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is full of suffering.

children.text: draṣṭā śrotā ca mantā ca |(kārya+karaṇam Ckāryaṃ* karaṇam )eva ca |
children.translated_text: A seer, a hearer, and a thinker, both agent and instrument—
conceiving 'I am this,' one revolves in <s>saṃsāra</s>.
By these causes, O wise one, the stream of birth flows forth;
from the absence of cause comes absence of effect—this you should understand.
Therein, one of right understanding, desiring liberation, should know the fourfold:
the awakened and the unawakened, the manifest and the unmanifest.
Having truly understood this fourfold, the knower of the field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>),
having abandoned the course of transmigration, attains the imperishable state.
For this purpose, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> in the world, expounders of the supreme <s>Brahman</s>,
practice <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibate studentship) here and cause <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> to dwell.

children.text: iti vākyam idaṃ* śrutvā |munes* tasya nṛ+pa+ātma+jaḥ |
children.translated_text: Having heard these words of that sage,

children.text: abhyupāyaṃ* ca papraccha |padam eva ca naiṣṭhikam ||12.43|
children.translated_text: the prince asked about the method and also the ultimate state:

children.text: brahma+caryam idaṃ* caryaṃ* |yathā yāvac* ca yatra ca |
children.translated_text: "This <s>brahmacarya</s> that is to be practiced—how, how long, and where?
And the limit of this <s>Dharma</s>—you should explain."
Then <s>Arāḍa</s>, according to his scripture, clearly and in summary,
expounded that very <s>Dharma</s> to him in another form:

children.text: ayam ādau gṛhān* muktvā |bhaikṣākaṃ* liṅgam āśritaḥ |
children.translated_text: "First, having left the household, one takes the mark of a mendicant,
and lives upholding moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>) that is extensive in its practice.

children.text: saṃtoṣaṃ* param āsthāya |yena tena yatas* tataḥ |
children.translated_text: Resorting to supreme contentment, from whatever, by whatever,
one frequents a secluded dwelling, free from pairs of opposites, learned in scripture, and skilled.

children.text: tato* rāgād* bhayaṃ* dṛṣṭvā |vairāgyāc* ca paraṃ* śivam |
children.translated_text: Then, having seen the danger in passion and the supreme good in dispassion,
restraining the aggregate of senses, one strives for the tranquility of the mind.
Then, secluded from desires and from ill-will and the rest,
one attains the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), born of seclusion, accompanied by deliberation.

children.text: tac* ca (dhyāna+sukhaṃ* Cdhyānaṃ* sukhaṃ* )prāpya |tat tad* eva vitarkayan |
children.translated_text: And having attained the happiness of that <s>dhyāna</s>, still deliberating upon that,
the foolish person is carried away by the acquisition of unprecedented happiness.
By such tranquility, which censures desire and hatred,
deceived by satisfaction, one attains the <s>Brahmaloka</s> (world of <s>Brahmā</s>).
But the wise one, knowing that deliberations cause disturbance of the mind,
attains the <s>dhyāna</s> free from them, accompanied by joy and happiness.

children.text: hriyamāṇas* tayā prītyā |yo* viśeṣaṃ* na paśyati |
children.translated_text: He who, carried away by that joy, does not perceive the distinction,

children.text: sthānaṃ* bhāsvaram āpnoti |deveṣv* (ābhāsvareṣu saḥ Cābhā+sureṣv* api )||12.53|
children.translated_text: attains a radiant station among the <s>Ābhāsvara</s> (radiant) gods.
But he who distinguishes the mind from joy and happiness—
he obtains the third <s>dhyāna</s>, happiness without joy.

children.text: yas* tu tasmin sukhe magno* |na viśeṣāya yatnavān |
children.translated_text: But he who, absorbed in that happiness, does not strive for distinction,
attains a happiness shared with the <s>Śubhakṛtsna</s> (All-Beautiful) deities.

children.text: tā+dṛśaṃ* sukham āsādya |yo* na (rajyaty* upekṣakaḥ Crajyann* upekṣate )|
children.translated_text: Having reached such happiness, he who does not become attached, remaining equanimous,
attains the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, free from both happiness and suffering.

children.text: tatra ke+cid* vyavasyanti |mokṣa* ity* (abhimāninaḥ Capi māninaḥ )|
children.translated_text: Some therein conclude that this is liberation, those who are proud,
because of the abandonment of happiness and suffering and the inactivity of the mind.

children.text: asya dhyānasya tu phalaṃ* |samaṃ* devair* bṛhat+phalaiḥ |
children.translated_text: But the fruit of this <s>dhyāna</s> is said to be equal to the <s>Bṛhatphala</s> (Great Fruit) gods;
those of great wisdom who examine say it lasts a great time.
Having arisen from that <s>samādhi</s>, and seeing the faults of embodied beings,
the wise one ascends to knowledge for the cessation of the body.
Then, abandoning that <s>dhyāna</s>, having determined upon distinction,

children.text: kāmebhya* iva (sa* prājño* Csat+prājño* )|rūpād* api virajyate ||12.60|
children.translated_text: that wise one becomes dispassionate even toward form, as toward desires.

children.text: śarīre khāni yāny* asmin |tāny* ādau parikalpayan |
children.translated_text: Contemplating first the apertures that exist in this body,
then even in solid substances, one comes to accept space.
Another wise one, having condensed the self that has become like space,
perceiving that same as infinite, attains distinction.
Yet another, skilled in what concerns the self, having turned the self by the self,
perceiving that there is 'nothing at all'—this is called <s>ākiṃcanya</s> (nothingness).
Then, like a reed drawn from its sheath, like a bird from a cage,
the knower of the field, having emerged from the body, is called 'liberated.'

children.text: etat tat paramaṃ* brahma |nir+liṅgaṃ* dhruvam a+kṣaram |
children.translated_text: This is that supreme <s>Brahman</s>, without marks, eternal, imperishable,
which the wise who know the truth call 'liberation.'"

children.text: ity* upāyaś* ca mokṣaś* ca |mayā saṃdarśitas* tava |
children.translated_text: "Thus the method and liberation have been shown to you by me;
if it is known, if it pleases, let it be properly undertaken."
"<s>Jaigīṣavya</s>, and <s>Janaka</s>,

children.text: imaṃ* panthānam āsādya |muktā* hy* anye ca mokṣiṇaḥ ||12.67|
children.translated_text: and the elder <s>Parāśara</s>—

children.text: iti tasya sa* tad* vākyaṃ* |gṛhītvā (tu Cna )vicārya ca |
children.translated_text: having attained this path, they were liberated, and other seekers of liberation too."
Having received and examined those words of his,

children.text: śrutaṃ* jñānam idaṃ* sūkṣmaṃ* |parataḥ parataḥ śivam |
children.translated_text: impelled by the force of his prior causes, he replied:
"This knowledge has been heard by me, subtle, increasingly auspicious,
but because of the non-abandonment of the knower of the field, I know this to be non-final.
For even though the knower of the field is liberated from the modifications and <s>Prakṛti</s>,

children.text: viśuddho* yady* api hy* ātmā |nirmukta* iti kalpyate |
children.translated_text: I consider it to have the nature of production, the very nature of a seed.
Even if the self is conceived as purified and liberated,
since conditions still exist, it will become bound again.

children.text: ((Crohati pratyayais* tais* tais* |tadvat so* *api mato* mama C))||12.72|
children.translated_text: Just as a seed does not sprout when deprived of season, soil, and water,
but sprouts when those conditions are present—so too, it seems to me.
And as for liberation being conceived through the abandonment of action, ignorance, and craving—
the complete abandonment of these does not exist as long as the self exists.

children.text: ātmanas* tu sthitir* yatra |tatra sūkṣmam idaṃ* trayam ||12.74|
children.translated_text: By progressive abandonment of these three, distinction is perceived;
but where the self persists, there this threefold remains, however subtle.
Because of the subtlety of the faults and the inactivity of the mind,
and because of the length of lifespan, liberation is merely imagined.
And as for the abandonment of ego-sense that is conceived—

children.text: saṃkhyā+ādibhir* a+muktaś* ca |nir+guṇo* na bhavaty* ayam |
children.translated_text: as long as the self exists, there is no abandonment of ego-sense.
Not liberated from number and the rest, this self does not become quality-less;

children.text: guṇino* hi guṇānāṃ* ca |vyatireko* na vidyate |
children.translated_text: therefore, in the absence of quality-lessness, liberation of this self cannot be affirmed.
For between the possessor of qualities and the qualities themselves, no real distinction exists;

children.text: prāg* dehān* na bhaved* dehī |prāg* guṇebhyas* tathā guṇī |
children.translated_text: fire, deprived of form and heat, is indeed not perceived.
Before the body, the embodied one would not exist; before the qualities, the possessor of qualities;

children.text: kṣetra+jño* vi+śarīraś* ca |jño* vā syād* a+jña* eva vā |
children.translated_text: then how, having been liberated first, is the embodied one bound again?

children.text: yadi jño* jñeyam asya*asti |jñeye sati na mucyate ||12.80|
children.translated_text: The knower of the field, being without body, would be either a knower or not a knower;

children.text: atha*a+jña* iti siddho* vaḥ |kalpitena kim ātmanā |
children.translated_text: if a knower, he has an object of knowledge; where an object of knowledge exists, he is not liberated.
But if it is established that he is a non-knower, then what need of a conceived self?

children.text: parataḥ paratas* tyāgo* |yasmāt tu guṇavān smṛtaḥ |
children.translated_text: For even without a self, non-knowledge is well-known, as in a log or a wall.
Since progressive abandonment is held to be meritorious,

children.text: iti dharmam arāḍasya |viditvā na tutoṣa saḥ |
children.translated_text: therefore I consider that complete accomplishment lies in the abandonment of everything.
Thus, having understood the <s>Dharma</s> of <s>Arāḍa</s>, he was not satisfied;
knowing it to be incomplete, he departed from there.

children.text: ātma+grāhāc* ca tasya*api |jagṛhe na sa* darśanam ||12.84|
children.translated_text: Then, wishing to hear a superior teaching, he went to the hermitage of <s>Udraka</s>;
and he did not accept his doctrine either, because of its clinging to a self.
For the sage <s>Udraka</s>, knowing the fault of both perception and non-perception,
beyond nothingness, attained the state characterized by neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
But since this subtle object of concentration, being neither perception nor non-perception,
is neither non-perceiving nor truly perceiving—therefore he had no desire for that.
And since the mind remains fixed there, not operating elsewhere,

children.text: yasmāc* ca (tad* Ctam )api prāpya |punar* āvartate jagat |
children.translated_text: being subtle and dull—therefore it is neither non-perception nor perception.
Since, having attained even that, the world revolves again,
the <s>Bodhisattva</s>, seeking the supreme, therefore abandoned <s>Udraka</s>.
Then, leaving his hermitage, seeking the good, with firm resolve,
he went to the hermitage called after the city of the royal sage <s>Gaya</s>.
Then, on the bank of the <s>Nairañjanā</s> river, that pure one of pure valor,
that sage, delighting in solitary dwelling, made his abode.
There previously, five monks, unsteady with sense-mastery,
practitioners of austerity and vows, he observed.
Those mendicant monks, seekers of liberation, attended upon him there upon seeing him,
like the sense-objects attending upon a lord who has acquired health and wealth through merit.
Being worshipped by those humble ones, who followed him through discipline,
who remained subject to his will as disciples, like the unsteady senses attending the mind—
thinking, 'This may be the means for ending death and birth,'
he then undertook difficult austerities through fasting.
Performing various fasting observances, difficult for men,
for six years, seeking tranquility, he produced emaciation in himself.
At mealtimes, with single jujube fruits, sesame seeds, and grains of rice,

children.text: dehād* apacayas* tena |tapasā tasya yaḥ kṛtaḥ |
children.translated_text: seeking to reach the far shore of the shoreless <s>saṃsāra</s>, he endured.
The diminution of his body wrought by that austerity
was again matched by the increase wrought by his radiance.
Though emaciated, not diminished in the splendor of his fame, he brought delight to the eyes of others,
like the autumn moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight to night-lotuses.
Reduced to nothing but skin and bones, with flesh, fat, and blood entirely gone,
though diminished, his depth was not diminished—he appeared like the ocean.
fearful of existence, he formed this resolve out of longing for <s>Buddhahood</s>. ||12.100|

children.text: na*ayaṃ* dharmo* virāgāya |na bodhāya na muktaye |
children.translated_text: "This method is not for dispassion, nor for enlightenment, nor for liberation;

children.text: jambu+mūle mayā prāpto* |yas* tadā sa* vidhir* dhruvaḥ ||12.101|
children.translated_text: what I attained beneath the <s>Jambu</s> tree that time—that method is the sure one. ||12.101|
And that cannot be attained by one who is weak"—thus, with renewed conviction,
for the sake of increasing bodily strength, he reflected further: ||12.102|
"Exhausted by hunger, thirst, and weariness, with a mind unsound from fatigue—
how can one who is not at ease attain the fruit that is to be attained by the mind? ||12.103|
<s>Nirvṛti</s> (inner peace) is properly attained through the constant nourishment of the senses;
through the state of nourished senses, soundness of mind is obtained. ||12.104|
For one whose mind is sound and clear, <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) arises;
for one whose mind is united with <s>samādhi</s>, the practice of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) proceeds. ||12.105|
Through the practice of <s>dhyāna</s>, those <s>dharmas</s> (states) are attained by which is reached

children.text: dur+labhaṃ* śāntam a+jaraṃ* |paraṃ* tad* a+mṛtaṃ* padam ||12.106|
children.translated_text: that hard-to-attain, peaceful, ageless, supreme, immortal state." ||12.106|
Therefore, "nourishment is the root of this method"—having firmly resolved thus,
the steadfast one of boundless wisdom, having made up his mind to take food, ||12.107|
having bathed, emerged slowly from the ford of the <s>Nairañjanā</s> river, thin and emaciated,
supported by the trees on the bank, whose branches bowed down reverentially, offering their hands. ||12.108|
Then the daughter of the chief cowherd, urged by the gods,
her heart overflowing with joy, came there—<s>Nandabalā</s> by name. ||12.109|
With arms bright as white conch, wearing a dark blue garment,
like the supreme river <s>Yamunā</s> with foam-garlanded dark waters, ||12.110|
she, with devotion-nourished joy, with lotus-eyes blossoming,
bowing her head before him, offered him rice-milk. ||12.111|
By partaking of it, having made her life fruitful,
he became capable of attaining <s>Bodhi</s>, with his six senses nourished. ||12.112|
With his body sufficiently nourished, the sage, with fitting and good renown,
bore alone the dual burden of beauty and steadfastness, shining like the moon and the ocean. ||12.113|

children.text: āvṛtta* iti vijñāya |taṃ* jahuḥ (pañca bhikṣavaḥ Cpañca+bhikṣavaḥ )|
children.translated_text: Knowing that he had turned back (from austerities), five <s>Bhikṣus</s> abandoned him,
as the five elements abandon the self when it is liberated. ||12.114|
Then, with resolve as his companion, he crossed the grassy ground
and went to the foot of an <s>Aśvattha</s> (Bodhi) tree, firm in his determination for enlightenment. ||12.115|
Then, at that time, with the stride of a king of elephants,
awakened by the incomparable sound of his footsteps,
confident that the great sage's enlightenment was assured,
<s>Kāla</s>, the supreme serpent, uttered a hymn of praise: ||12.116|
"As the earth groans again and again, pressed by your feet, O sage,
as the earth resounds,

children.text: yathā ca te rājati sūryavat prabhā |
children.translated_text: and as your radiance blazes forth like the sun—

children.text: dhruvaṃ* tvam iṣṭaṃ* phalam adya bhokṣyase ||12.117|
children.translated_text: surely today you shall enjoy the desired fruit. ||12.117|
As flocks of crows wheeling in the sky
circle you clockwise, O lotus-eyed one,

children.text: yathā ca saumyā* divi vānti vāyavas* |
children.translated_text: and as gentle breezes blow in the sky—
you shall surely become a <s>Buddha</s> today." ||12.118|
Then, having been praised by that foremost serpent,
having gathered clean grass from a grass-cutter,
having made his vow, he sat down for enlightenment,
having resorted to the root of a great, pure tree. ||12.119|
Then he bound the supreme, unshakeable cross-legged posture,
compact as the coils of a sleeping serpent:
"I shall not break this seat upon the earth
until I have achieved my purpose." ||12.120|
Then the celestial beings felt incomparable joy;
(continued)
the herds of wild animals did not cry out, nor did the birds;
the forest trees, though struck by the wind, did not rustle,
when the Blessed One, firm in resolve, had taken his seat. ||12.121|
Thus ends the twelfth canto, named 'The Visit to <s>Arāḍa</s>,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>. |12|
Thirteenth Canto |13|
When that great sage, born of the lineage of royal sages,
had made his vow for liberation,
and sat there, the world rejoiced,
but <s>Māra</s>, the enemy of the true <s>Dharma</s>, was afraid. ||13.1|
He whom the world calls <s>Kāmadeva</s> (god of desire),
with his colorful weapons and flower-arrows,
that very lord of the dominion of desire—
they call him <s>Māra</s>, the foe of liberation. ||13.2|
His daughters, born of himself—Confusion, Delight, and Pride—
and three maidens—Discontent, Pleasure, and Craving—
asked him the cause of his mind's disturbance;

children.text: sa* tāṃś* ca tāś* ca*eva vaco* (*abhyuvāca Cbabhāṣe )||13.3|
children.translated_text: and he spoke these words to them all: ||13.3|
"That sage, wearing the armor of resolve,
having drawn the bow of wisdom with the arrow of truth,
sits desiring to conquer my domains;
therefore this despondency of my mind. ||13.4|

children.text: yadi hy* asau mām abhibhūya yāti |
children.translated_text: For if he conquers me and goes beyond,
and proclaims to the world the path of liberation,
then this domain of mine is today empty—
like that of the lord of <s>Videha</s> when fallen from his state. ||13.5|
Therefore, while he has not yet obtained the eye (of wisdom),
while he still remains in my domain,
I shall go to break his vow,
as a swollen river-current breaks a dam." ||13.6|
Then, taking up his bow made of flowers
and his five arrows that produce the delusion of the world,
he went to the foot of the <s>Aśvattha</s> tree with his sons,
he who causes unease in the minds of beings. ||13.7|
Then, to the tranquil sage seated on his seat,
desiring to cross to the other shore of the ocean of existence,
placing his left hand on the tip of his weapon,
playing with his arrow, <s>Māra</s> spoke thus: ||13.8|
"Arise, ho! O <s>Kṣatriya</s>, you who fear death!
Follow your own <s>Dharma</s>, abandon the <s>Dharma</s> of liberation!
Having subdued the world with arrows and sacrifices,
attain the realm of <s>Vāsava</s> (<s>Indra</s>)! ||13.9|
For this is the glorious path to advancement
that was followed by the earliest kings;
for one born in the vast lineage of royal sages,
this resort to begging is inglorious. ||13.10|
But if today you will not rise, O firm-souled one,
then be steady—do not release your vow!

children.text: mayā*udyato* hy* eṣa* śaraḥ sa* eva |
children.translated_text: For this is the very arrow raised by me
that was released against <s>Śūrpaka</s> (or <s>Sūryaka</s>), the foe of the fish. ||13.11|
Even <s>Aiḍa</s> (<s>Purūravas</s>), barely touched by it,
grandson of <s>Soma</s>, became distracted;
and <s>Śāntanu</s> too lost his self-control—
what then of a weakling in this degenerate age? ||13.12|
Therefore, rise quickly! Regain your senses!
For this arrow stands ready, licking its lips;
among those subject to their beloveds, devoted to pleasure—
I do not release it even against <s>Cakravāka</s> birds." ||13.13|
But when, though thus addressed, the <s>Śākya</s> sage, without attachment,
did not at all break his seat,
<s>Māra</s> released his arrow at him,

children.text: kanyāś* ca kṛtvā purataḥ sutāṃś* ca ||13.14|
children.translated_text: placing his daughters and sons before him. ||13.14|
But even when that arrow was released,
he paid it no heed and did not waver from his firmness;
seeing him thus, <s>Māra</s> was dejected
and, consumed with anxiety, spoke slowly: ||13.15|
"He by whom even the god <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) was pierced
and became agitated, on account of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains—

children.text: na cintayaty* eṣa* tam eva (bāṇaṃ* Cvāṇaṃ* )|
children.translated_text: this one does not even think about that very arrow;

children.text: kiṃ* syād* a+citto* na śaraḥ sa* eṣaḥ ||13.16|
children.translated_text: can he be without a mind? Or is it not the same arrow? ||13.16|
Therefore he does not deserve the flower-arrow,
nor enticement, nor the employment of passion;
he deserves from my fierce troops of demons
intimidation, threats, and blows." ||13.17|
<s>Māra</s> then remembered his own army,
wishing to create an obstacle to the <s>Śākya</s> sage's tranquility;
and his followers of various forms pressed around,
bearing spears, trees, javelins, clubs, and swords in hand. ||13.18|
With faces of boars, fish, horses, donkeys, and camels,
with faces of tigers, bears, lions, and elephants,
one-eyed, many-faced, three-headed,
pot-bellied and spotted-bellied, ||13.19|
some with knees fused to their thighs, with pot-shaped knees,
with tusks for weapons and claws for weapons,
with skull-faces, with many forms,
with half-shattered faces and huge mouths, ||13.20|
ash-red, mottled with red drops,
with skull-staves in hand, with yellow-grey hair,
with hanging garlands, with ears drooping like elephants',
some clad in hides and some naked, ||13.21|
half-white of face, half-green of body,
copper, smoky, tawny, and black,
with serpents draped as upper garments,
with girdles clanging with jangling bells, ||13.22|
tall as palm trees, bearing tridents,
terrible with fangs, and small as children,
with faces of rams and eyes of birds,
with cat-faces on human bodies, ||13.23|
with hair disheveled, crested, or half-shaved,
wearing red garments or tangled wrappings,
with gleeful faces and scowling faces,
some stealing splendor and some stealing the mind. ||13.24|
Some, advancing, leaped violently;
others jumped upon one another;
some sported in the sky,
and some roamed on the treetops. ||13.25|
One danced, whirling a trident;
one brandished a club, thundering;
one bellowed with delight like a bull;
one blazed from every pore of his body. ||13.26|
Such hosts of demons on all sides
surrounded that seat of enlightenment and stood there,
eager to seize and eager to slay,
awaiting the command of their lord. ||13.27|
Seeing the battle-hour of <s>Māra</s>
and of that bull of the <s>Śākyas</s> in the first watch of the night,
the sky did not shine, the earth trembled,
and the quarters blazed with sound. ||13.28|
The wind blew in all directions with violent force,

children.text: tārā* na rejur* na babhau śaśa+aṅkaḥ |
children.translated_text: the stars did not gleam, the moon did not shine,

children.text: tamaś* ca bhūyo* (vitatāna rātriḥ Cvitatāra rātreḥ )|
children.translated_text: and the night spread yet deeper darkness,
and all the oceans were agitated. ||13.29|
The great <s>Nāgas</s>, devoted to <s>Dharma</s>, bearers of the earth,
unable to bear the obstruction of the great sage,
with eyes turned in anger toward <s>Māra</s>,
they sighed and trembled. ||13.30|
But the divine sages, dwelling in purity,
engaged for the attainment of the true <s>dharma</s>,
mentally extended compassion toward <s>Māra</s>,
but did not go to anger, due to their dispassionate nature. ||13.31|
Seeing that root of <s>bodhi</s> (enlightenment) overrun
by that army of <s>Māra</s>, violent in nature,
there was a cry of 'Alas!' in the sky
from the <s>dharma</s>-minded ones who desired the liberation of the world. ||13.32|
But seeing the army of <s>Māra</s> stationed there,
obstructing the observance of <s>dharma</s>, the great sage
was neither agitated nor underwent any change,
like a lion seated among cows. ||13.33|
<s>Māra</s> then commanded his aroused army of spirits
to terrify him;

children.text: svaiḥ svaiḥ prabhāvair* atha sā*asya senā |
children.translated_text: and that army, each with their own powers,
set their minds to breaking his steadfastness. ||13.34|
Some stood swaying, with many dangling tongues,
with sharp, fierce fangs, with tawny-ringed eyes,
with gaping mouths, with ears like fixed pegs,
standing there, as if to terrify. ||13.35|
Before those standing there, of such a kind,
terrible in form and in disposition,
the great sage neither trembled nor was alarmed,
as if before children at play, acting wildly. ||13.36|
Then one, with eyes rolling in fury,
raised a club to strike him;
but his arm with the club froze stiff,
like that of <s>Indra</s> of old with his <s>vajra</s> (thunderbolt). ||13.37|
Some, having lifted rocks and trees,
were unable to hurl them at the sage;
they fell, trees, rocks and all,
like the foothills of the <s>Vindhya</s>, shattered by the <s>vajra</s>. ||13.38|
Rocks, trees, and axes, hurled by some

children.text: śilāś* ca vṛkṣāś* ca paraśvadhāś* ca |
children.translated_text: who had leapt into the sky,
remained suspended in the sky and did not fall,
like multicolored bases of twilight clouds. ||13.39|
Another hurled at him a blazing
firebrand as large as a mountain peak,
which, as soon as released, while still in the sky,
burst into a hundred pieces by his power. ||13.40|
Another, blazing like the sun risen from the sky,
released a great shower of embers,
and fragments of golden caverns,
like Mount <s>Meru</s> ablaze at the end of a <s>kalpa</s> (aeon). ||13.41|
But that shower of embers, with sparks,
raining down upon the root of <s>bodhi</s>,
through the abiding in <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) of that best of sages,
became a shower of red lotus petals. ||13.42|
Though assailed thus with afflictions of body and mind,
by such attacks as these being rained down,
the <s>Śākya</s> sage did not stir from his seat,
as if embracing his resolve as a kinsman. ||13.43|
Then others vomited serpents from their mouths,
as from decayed trees;
but those serpents, as if bound by <s>mantras</s>, near him,
neither breathed, nor moved, nor stirred. ||13.44|
Others, becoming great storm clouds,
with lightning and fierce thundering crashes,
released a shower of stones upon that tree,
but it became a beautiful shower of flowers. ||13.45|
Then an arrow placed upon a bow by another
blazed right there but did not fly;
like the anger of a resentful man who is powerless,
smoldering within himself. ||13.46|
Five arrows discharged by another
remained in the sky and did not fall upon the sage,
like the five senses of an examiner
who fears <s>saṃsāra</s>, when directed toward sense objects. ||13.47|
Another, enraged, rushed forward with intent to kill,
seizing a mace, facing the great sage;
but he fell helpless, his purpose unaccomplished,
like one of the world, into harmful faults. ||13.48|
A woman, dark as a cloud, skull in hand,
to confuse the mind of the great sage,
roamed about there erratically, never standing still,
like the intellect of a fickle person regarding the scriptures. ||13.49|
One, having fixed a blazing gaze,
wishing to burn him with the fire of his eyes, as with a serpent's venom,
gazed at the sage seated right there,
like a desire-natured one looking at the good that has been taught. ||13.50|
Another, straining to lift a heavy boulder,
exhausted himself in vain, his effort frustrated,
like one who desires to attain <s>dharma</s>, accessible through <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) and <s>samādhi</s> (concentration),
through bodily toil alone. ||13.51|
Others, in the forms of hyenas and lions,
uttered loud, great roars,
by which all creatures shrank on every side,
thinking that the sky, struck by the <s>vajra</s>, was splitting. ||13.52|
Deer and elephants, uttering cries of distress,
both fled and hid;
and in that night, from all directions as if in daytime,
birds flew about, crying in distress. ||13.53|
But by such cries as those,
though all beings were terrified,
the sage neither feared nor shrank,
like <s>Garuḍa</s> at the cawing of crows. ||13.54|
The more the sage did not fear
those terror-inspiring hosts,
the more the foe of the bearers of <s>dharma</s>,
<s>Māra</s>, sank under grief and rage. ||13.55|
Then a certain being, of invisible form,
of superior nature, standing in the sky,
seeing the sage wronged though he bore no enmity,
addressed <s>Māra</s> in a great voice: ||13.56|
'O <s>Māra</s>, you should not exert yourself in vain;
abandon your violent nature and go in peace;
for this one cannot be shaken by you,
any more than the great mountain <s>Meru</s> by the wind. ||13.57|
Fire might perhaps abandon its heat,
water its fluidity, earth its firmness,
but this one, whose meritorious deeds were accumulated over countless <s>kalpas</s>,

children.text: na tv* eva jahyād* vyavasāyam eṣaḥ ||13.58|
children.translated_text: would never abandon his determination. ||13.58|

children.text: yo* niścayo* hy* asya parākramaś* ca |
children.translated_text: For this resolve of his, and his valor,

children.text: tejaś* ca yad* yā ca dayā prajāsu |
children.translated_text: and the brilliance, and the compassion for beings that is his —
without attaining the truth, he will not rise,
just as the thousand-rayed sun will not rise without dispelling darkness. ||13.59|
One obtains fire by rubbing wood,
and finds water by digging the earth;

children.text: nirbandhinaḥ kiṃ+(cana na*asty* a+sādhyaṃ* Cca na na*asya sādhyaṃ* )|
children.translated_text: for one who persists, nothing is unattainable;

children.text: nyāyena yuktaṃ* ca kṛtaṃ* ca sarvam ||13.60|
children.translated_text: everything rightly undertaken is accomplished. ||13.60|
Therefore, having compassion for the afflicted world,
which abides in the diseases of passion and the rest,
this great physician should not be obstructed,
as he labors for the remedy of knowledge. ||13.61|
And when the world is led astray by many wrong paths,
he who seeks the right path with effort —
it is not proper to disturb that guide,
like a good guide when the caravan has gone astray. ||13.62|
When beings are lost in the great darkness,
this lamp of knowledge is being kindled;
it is not noble to extinguish it,
like a lamp being lit in the darkness. ||13.63|
And seeing the world sunk in the great flood of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
finding no shore,
what noble person would think of evil

children.text: (kaś* cintayet Ckaś+cin* nayet )tasya tu pāpam āryaḥ ||13.64|
children.translated_text: toward one who has undertaken to rescue it? ||13.64|
With patience as its sword, with steadfastness as its deep-set root,
with good conduct as its flower, with mindfulness and wisdom as its branches,
this tree of knowledge, which grants the fruit of <s>dharma</s>,
should not be uprooted while it is growing. ||13.65|
He whose wisdom is set on liberating the world,
bound in the mind by the firm nooses of delusion —
your desire to harm him is unfitting,
one who toils for the cause of freeing the world from its bonds. ||13.66|
For the deeds done by him for the sake of <s>bodhi</s> —
the appointed time for their fruition is now today;
he is seated in this place
just as the former sages were before him. ||13.67|
For this is the navel of the surface of the earth,
joined to the supreme power in its entirety;
there is no other spot on earth
that could sustain the force of his <s>samādhi</s>. ||13.68|

children.text: tan* mā kṛthāḥ śokam upehi śāntiṃ* |
children.translated_text: Therefore, do not grieve; approach peace;

children.text: mā bhūn* mahimnā tava māra mānaḥ |
children.translated_text: let there be no arrogance in you, O <s>Māra</s>, on account of your glory;
for prosperity, being unstable, is not to be trusted;
do you take pride in a tottering position?' ||13.69|

children.text: tataḥ sa* saṃśrutya ca tasya tad* vaco* |
children.translated_text: Then, having heard those words
and having witnessed the unshakable composure of the great sage,
<s>Māra</s> departed, his spirit crushed, his efforts destroyed,
with those arrows by which the minds of the world are struck. ||13.70|
Their joy gone, their effort rendered fruitless,
having dropped their rocks, firebrands, and trees,
his army fled in all directions,
like the army of an enemy when their refuge has been destroyed by a foe. ||13.71|
As the flower-bannered <s>Māra</s> fled with his followers, defeated,
and as the great sage triumphed, with darkness conquered, his nature spotless,

children.text: yuvatir* iva sa+hāsā dyauś* cakāśe sa+candrā |
children.translated_text: the sky shone forth with the moon, as if smiling like a young woman,
and there fell from the heavens a fragrant, water-laden shower of flowers. ||13.72|
And when the Evil One was vanquished and had departed,
the directions cleared, the moon shone forth,
from the sky there fell upon the earth showers of flowers,
and the night, free from stain, shone like a beautiful woman.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, entitled 'The Defeat of <s>Māra</s>,' in the great poem <s>Buddhacarita</s>, composed by <s>Aśvaghoṣa</s>. |13|
Canto Fourteen |14|

children.text: tato* māra+balaṃ* jitvā |dhairyeṇa ca śamena ca |
children.translated_text: Then, having conquered the army of <s>Māra</s> through steadfastness and tranquility,
wishing to know the supreme truth,
he meditated, skilled in <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation). ||14.1|
Having attained the supreme mastery in all the methods of <s>dhyāna</s>,
in the first watch of the night
he recalled the succession of his former births. ||14.2|

children.text: smṛtvā janma ca mṛtyuṃ* ca |tāsu tāsu*upapattiṣu |
children.translated_text: 'In that place I was this one, of such a name; having fallen from there, I came here' —
thus he recalled thousands of births, as if experiencing them again. ||14.3|
Having recalled birth and death in each of those existences,
then, compassionate of nature, he felt compassion for all beings. ||14.4|
'Having abandoned one's own family in this existence, and then performing deeds again elsewhere — this world, without a protector, revolves like a wheel indeed.' ||14.5|
Thus, as he recalled, for that one of controlled mind, there arose the firm conviction: '<s>saṃsāra</s> is without essence, like the pith of a plantain.' ||14.6|
But when the second watch arrived, he, of matchless valor,
obtained the supreme divine eye, the foremost among all who possess sight. ||14.7|
Then with that divine, perfectly purified eye,
he beheld the entire world as in a spotless mirror. ||14.8|
As he beheld beings of inferior and superior deeds,
their falling away and their rebirth, his compassionate nature grew. ||14.9|
"These beings of evil deeds go to bad destinies;
these others, of meritorious deeds, are established in the triple heaven. ||14.10|
Those born in the fearful, exceedingly terrible hells
are pitiably tormented by many kinds of suffering. ||14.11|
Some are made to drink boiling molten iron, glowing like fire;
others, screaming, are impaled upon red-hot iron stakes. ||14.12|
Some are cooked head-downward in iron cauldrons, like flour;
some are pitiably burned in blazing heaps of coals. ||14.13|
Some are devoured by fierce dogs with sharp iron fangs;
some by bold, iron-beaked crows, as if made of iron. ||14.14|
Some, wearied by burning, longing for cool shade,

children.text: asi+(pattra+vanaṃ* Cpatraṃ* vanaṃ* )nīlaṃ* |baddhā* iva viśanty* amī ||14.15|
children.translated_text: enter, as if bound, the dark forest of sword-leaf trees. ||14.15|
Some are split like timber by axes, their arms bound;
yet they do not perish even in agony, their lives sustained by their <s>karma</s>. ||14.16|

children.text: sukhaṃ* syād* iti yat karma |kṛtaṃ* duḥkha+nivṛttaye |
children.translated_text: The deed that was done for the removal of suffering, thinking 'this will bring happiness' —
the fruit of that is experienced helplessly as suffering alone. ||14.17|
Those who committed unwholesome deeds for the sake of happiness,

children.text: āsvādaḥ sa* kim eteṣāṃ* |karoti sukham aṇv* api ||14.18|
children.translated_text: and who are now grievously tormented — does that former taste bring them even the slightest happiness? ||14.18|
The impure deed that was done laughingly by those of impure souls —
that is experienced with weeping when the time of its ripening comes. ||14.19|
If those of sinful deeds could see the fruit of their actions,
they would vomit hot blood, as if struck in their vital parts. ||14.20|
"Even more than the bodily sufferings of hell,

These others, by various deeds born from the stirrings of the mind,
are born as suffering beings in the diverse realm of animal birth. ||14.21|
For the sake of flesh, skin, hair, and teeth, or from enmity, or from madness,
they are pitiably slaughtered here, even as their kinsmen watch. ||14.22|
Unable, helpless, tormented by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion,
they are driven as oxen and horses, their bodies wounded by goads. ||14.23|
Even those who are strong, born as elephants, are driven by the weak,
their heads afflicted by the hook, struck by heels and spurs. ||14.24|

children.text: satsv* apy* anyeṣu duḥkheṣu |duḥkhaṃ* yatra viśeṣataḥ |
children.translated_text: Though there are other sufferings too, the special suffering here
is from mutual hostility and from subjugation to others. ||14.25|
Those dwelling in the sky are harassed by sky-dwellers; those in the water by water-creatures;
those on land by land-dwellers — and each is preyed upon by the others. ||14.26|
And these others, born with minds overwhelmed by jealousy,
pitiably experience their fruit in the lightless world of the <s>Pitṛs</s> (ancestors). ||14.27|
With mouths as narrow as the eye of a needle and bellies as vast as mountains,
these unfortunate ones are tormented by sufferings born of hunger and thirst. ||14.28|
Sustained by hope, upheld by their own <s>karma</s>,
